MACDONELL (South Toronto) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 22) to amend the Dominion Elections Act. He said: The Bill is a repetition of a Bill that I introduced last session. It has two provisions. One is to dispense with the $200 deposit now necessary to be made by a candidate. The other asks that the general election day throughout Canada be made a public holiday.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Mr. MACDONELL moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 23) to amend the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, 1907. He said: This Bill is a copy of the Bill which I introduced towards the close of last session, and time was not afforded to reach a conclusion upoh it. Its object is to amend the Industrial Disputes Act in several more or less important respects. First, it asks that the authority which the Act now requires to be obtained from a labour union desiring to strike, in the shape of a meeting, and the proceedings consequent thereon in the way of notice, &c., &c., be dispensed with. That is found expensive and cumbersome, and not conducive to the best working out of the Act. The next provision deals with the fees that are payable to the arbitrators. I have not inserted any fees here, leaving the amount to be considered by the government. At present the chairman receives a larger fee than the other members of the board, although he performs no greater service. The present fee is $15 per day. It is thought that a general charge of $25 per day for every member of the board would be reasonable, especially in view of the fact that most of the sittings are continued well on into the night. A further amendment is proposed to section 57 of the Act, which provides that only investigations regarding intended changes in wages and hours of labour can take place. It is desired that these should be extended to any conditions affecting employment. Then, at present the onus of proceeding with an investigation does not rest on anybody. That is found to work hardship, and the provision of the Bill is that on those who set the Act in motion by giving notice of a desire or intention to effect a change in working conditions, shall rest the onus of proceeding with the appointment of the board of arbitrators, and that no change in the conditions shall take place after the notice is given. At present the conditions can be changed by either party up to the time the board is appointed. That is found to work hardship, certain interested parties taking advantage of the delay between the serving of the notice and the appointment of the board to change the conditions of labour. The spirit of the Act is that no change in the conditions of labour shall take place after the notice is once given, when the parties are at arms length and the issue is on.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Mr. MACDONELL moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 24) to amend the Rail-9
way Act. He said: This is to amend section 341. The lion. Minister of Railways recollects that during last session, when his general Bill was moved to the House, I sought to have adopted then the amendment I now propose. Under section 77, no discrimination is allowed a railway company, and section 341 gives the company the right to issue family commutation and other cheap rate tickets. The question has arisen, both before the Railway Commission and in the courts, as regards the right of a railway company to discriminate against a locality by withholding the issue of these cheap rate tickets in any locality, and it is to make the matter clearer and prevent discrimination against localities or persons that I introduce this Bill. The Railway Commission have considered that there is a conflict between section 341 and section 77, and the Act should be amended so as to make it clear.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

WARBURTON (Queens, P.E. I.) moved for:
A copy of all memorials, reports, correspondence and documents in the possession .if the government not already brought down, relating to a survey of a route for a tunnel under the Straits of Northumberland between the province of Prince Edward Island and
the mainland of Canada, and also relating to the construction of such tunnel.
He said : Mr Speaker, this is a question which has been often brought before the parliament of Canada, although it has not been presented during the present parliament until now. Last year, owing to the fact that there was a serious falling off in the revenues of the country, I did not myself consider it an opportune time to move a resolution which if adopted might mean the expenditure of a considerable sum of money, and consequently I deemed it better to wait for a more convenient time when the revenues of the country would be buoyant and when those in charge of the finances might be in a more melting frame of mind and better prepared to give the people of Prince Edward Island assistance in this direction. At all events the question has been ventilated in the press and in parliament for years. Permit me to say that in my humble opinion the method adopted by some of its advocates, and the press, particularly in the press of Prince Edward Island, has not been characterized by that common sense which would have been better for the tunnel. We have had speeches on the hustings and editorials in the newspapers which have brought ridicule upon a worthy scheme and which to some extent at least has made it a laughing stock. In consequence of this I find it more difficult to remove the wrong impressions created by the absurd declarations which have been made by would be advocates of the scheme, than in gaining the sympathy of those in parliament and outside of parliament when I submit facts. As you were aware, Mr. Speaker, some 19 years ago the government of Sir John Macdonald to.ok steps towards getting a survey of that part of the Straits of Northumberland where this tunnel is to be built. So far as that survey ivent it was useful, but it did not go far enough and was so imperfect that it would be quite impossible for any one to tender for the construction of a tunnel on the data which it furnished. The survey was made by a Mr. Palmer, of England, who was said to be an expert in this branch of engineering. I met Mr. Palmer in those days in Prince Edw'ard Island, and whatever the cause of it was there seemed to be a great deal of friction between him and those who were then actively interesting themselves in the project. However that was, the survey was not made to the extent we had expected. Possibly we were looking for too much and possibly, and very likely, our imperfect knowledge of that sort of'work did not enable us to form a just estimate of the extent of survey that should be accomplished for the sum of money appropriated for it. Of course, I recognize that laymen are apt to he led astray when they come to con-

sider questions which require great engineering skill. However, upon the information reported to him by Mr. Palmer's survey, Sir Douglas Fox made a very important report. It does not require any words from me to add to the fame of Sir Douglas Fox as a great engineer. I shall, with the permission of the House, read certain extracts from the report of Sir Douglas Fox and from the correspondence with the late Senator Howlan, and I shall read these extracts in order to explain to the House perhaps more fully than has been explained in any former discussion the position which is taken by a great many of the people of Prince Edward Island and the mainland, and the position which I myself take now.
Sir Douglas, in the opening of his report, gives us this information. He said:
,Tlie greatest depth of water is shown as being 96 feet at high water, with a rise of tides of six feet at springs and three feet at neap, and the speed of the current as not exceeding three knots, with two hours of slack water each tide.
The distance from shore to shore is given as about 13,200 lineal yards, or say from shaft to shaft 13,500 lineal yards, exclusive of land approaches on either side, of which about 2,000 lineal yards would be in the tunnel.
Mr. Palmer further reports that the shores upon either coast are well adapted for railway approaches, varying from 15 to 35 feet in height above high water mark, with a mean altitude of 25 feet, the soil being of a red clayey nature. It appears also that the higher land on Prince Edward Island shore falls away towards the interior which will, therefore, shorten the approaches on that side.
That section of the report bears more upon the nature of the particular material through which the proposed tunnel would run. Then he took up the question of the stratification, upon which he reported as follows:
Upon the all important question of stratification on the proposed alignment, Mr. Palmer quotes the following opinion, given him verbally by Mr. Francis Bain on the occasion of his visit:-
Mr. Bain was a somewhat noted geologist in that section of the country

' In his belief, a bed of red clay shale, varying in thickness from 50 to 80 feet extends right across the Straits of Northumberland. It lies almost horizontally upon a carboniferous or gray sandstone base, and is said to contain small occasional lenticular masses of fine red sandstone.'
Mr. Palmer adds, as the result of his own investigation :	' The geological outcrop on
either shore in which the strata are distinctly visible, the formation of the surrounding country, the stratification seen in neighbouring wells, combined with the opinion of Mr. Bain, the geologist who is a native of the island, and has a knowledge of its entire formation, proves that a most favourable and impervious stratum does exist for subaqueous tunneling.

What is the distance?

The distance under water is not more than seven and a half miles. It has been customary in correspondence and newspaper articles and in discussions on the floor of this House to quote letters written by the late Sir John Macdonald and the right hon. the leader of this House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) as well as speeches by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden), the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) and others. I must frankly say that I have never been able to see a great deal of force in quoting speeches or letters of that kind. They are valuable to this extent that they show the good feeling of these hon. gentlemen and their willingness to help us; but however eminent these hon. gentlemen may be, however high they may stand in the service of their country and in the confidence of their respective parties, and however eminent they may be m the history of the country, such quotations are not "the best way in which to impress this matter upon the attention of the government and the House. I have long come to the conclusion that the strongest argument one can use on behalf of any public work is the argument that it is for the best advantage of Canada, I do not think it wise to argue on purely sectional grounds and say:	I
want this thing for my province because it is my province. For my part I want this tunnel, not only because it will be to the advantage of Prince Edward Island, but to Canada as a whole. Anything that tends to the consolidation of this Dominion tends to its welfare as a whole. Anything that tends, for example, to unite the island of Vancouver with the main land by material as well as theoretical bonds, by permanent and continuous bonds, does to that extent -and it is to a very considerable extent- strengthen the bonds that unite the various parts of our nation. On that ground, I urge this matter on the attention of the government and the House. You cannot exnect Canada as a whole to be contented and progressive so long as there is a festering sore in any part of it. Every day we hear of applications to the government for assistance to improve transportation facilities in various parts of the country. In many cases these improvements will be confined to certain provinces, but nevertheless, they have a great bearing on the general prosperity of the country. Canada is now building the great transcontinental. That railway will be of very little practical use Mr. WARBTJRTON.
to us down in Prince Edward Island, yet four or five years ago, I went to defeat on that question and am prepared to go to defeat on it again-not because the railway is of much use to us in Prince Edward Island but because it will bind together the various parts of the country and make of us one nation. The greatest question before the country and to-day is that of consolidation, and transportation is the largest element in that respect. In the speech of His Excellency, he mentions the proposed road to Hudson bay. That road will be soon undertaken ana built. It will be of no earthly use to us in Prince Edward Island but will be of great benefit to our fellow Canadians in the west by enabling them to get their produce to market more expeditiously and cheaper, and for that reason, although the road is of no benefit to my constituency, I shall give the project my support. Then there is the proposed expenditure on the Welland canal. It is important to the trade of Montreal and the west that the Welland canal should be deepened and broadened. Although we in Prince Edward Island are outside the track and influence of that canal and can derive no great benefit from it, I am going to support the project for the reasons I have given.
I have here a summary of a speech de-livefed by the Minister "of Railways at Stayner, in February, 1908, which appeared in newspapers, and in which he spoke of the Trent Valley canal. I do not propose to give his speech in extenso, but merely a brief summary to this effect:	The Minister of Railways defended the spending of money for transportation facilities because the people in that way obtained higher prices for their products. The price of products he added, was governed largely by the speed with which they could be got to market. When the transcontinental railways were completed, he said, the country would still not have sufficient transportation. Again dealing with the Trent Valley canal project, he said the country had been long committed to that scheme and the present government had said it would be built. He added:
If I stay where I am as Minister of Railways I am going to build that canal through to the Georgian bay.
He also referred to the building of better storage facilities on the eastern side of the Georgian bay and elsewhere where they were needed. I think he might have gone further and added a number of other works for the benefit of Canada, not that they are of benefit to Prince Edward Island, had they been brought to his mind.
It is this question of transportation to which the minister so well referred that affects us. We have a very fertile part of of Canada. We have very little poor land on the island; I suppose it is not as fertile

as the more fertile parts of Manitoba, Alberta or Saskatchewan, but taking the average of those provinces it is quite as fertile, and we have very little land that is not fertile. Our land is very nearly all owned by farmers, it is worked by the farmers and their families, and they raise an enormous quantity of produce on - those farms. Our population is from 45 to 50 per square mile, arid we require facilities not only for freight' traffic, but also for passenger traffic. We do not complain about the summer facilities; we do not mind crossing over the Straits in the summer, but we do object to getting stuck in the ice in the winter as we have done in the past. If we could manage to get a line of steamers crossing over in winter that would keep navigation open throughout the season-and this I believe to be possible, as I shall endeavour to demonstrate to the House on a future occasion-we would not complain, but I am assuming that the winter conditions will continue as they have been and that we will still be exposed to the danger of having to cross the Straits on the small ice boats. It is for that reason that I am bringing this matter before the House to-day. I wish to commend it to the consideration of the government. As you can see it is not a very difficult matter to give us this service. I am not asking the government to build the tunnel, I am merely asking them to take such measures as will show whether or not it is practicable to build the tunnel. I am simply asking that the preliminaries shall be carried out in order to enable us or any other practical man to judge what can be done or ought to be done. I do not think this is asking too much. I feel sure that in this matter we will have the sympathy of members on both sides of the House. If they can see their way clear to assist us in this matter I have confidence that they will do so and therefore, without taking more of your time, I shall move the resolution standing in my name.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. RICHARDS (Prince, Prince Edward Island).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to say a few words in support of the motion made by my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. Warburton). The question of transportation between Prince Edward Island and the mainland is of great importance to the people of that province. This position I think will be generally admitted at least by those who are familiar with the conditions which exist in that part of Canada. It is true that our means of communication in the winter season have been greatly improved of late years by reason of our having steamers generally capable of breaking the ice in the winter season. The present administration have done a great deal in that regard; they have put on the ' Minto,' a powerful boat which has done very good service;
and recently a new boat called the * Earl Grey,' costing something like $500,000 has been put upon that service. It remains to be seen how far she will be successful in keeping up continuous communication during the winter. We have every reason to believe from the pains taken in the construction of that boat and from her great power and improved design, incorporating the latest improvements with regard to breaking ice, that she will do a great deal to keep up communication in a more regular way than has been possible in the past. However, during a very severe winter, and *we have these occasionally, I am of the opinion that it would be very difficult for any boat, no matter how powerful she may be or what her design, to keep up regular communication in winter and for this reason we are looking fox some means by which continuous communication can be maintained.
It is not necessary for me to repeat what my hon. friend (Mr. Warburton) has said with regard to estimates and opinions that have been published by so eminent an authority as Sir Douglas Fox. It is beyond question that since he made that estimate the science of tunnelling has advanced greatly, and to-day the work of constructing a tunnel can be done at a much lower cost than would have been possible fifteen or twenty years ago. Tunnelling is not a new thing. In the State of New York there are tunnels of great length and in- Ontario large tunnels are also to be found. Tunnelling is practicable in other parts and I have no doubt that it would be practicable between Prince Edward Island and the mainland of Canada.
Prince Edward Island, as many of you are aware, is a very fertile little province. As has been stated, it has a larger population to the square mile than perhaps any other province in the Dominion. We have a large export trade, and what has been done in giving us winter steamers has greatly increased our winter trade, so that our exports during the winter months are nearly as large as they are during the summer, and for this reason there is great necessity for having some better means of transportation. I shall not go into particulars as to the size of this tunnel or other features that have been touched on by my hon. friend, but shall simply say that we want to know whether or not the construction of such a tunnel is practicable and that we think the time has arrived when this question should be settled one way or the other. To my mind the only way in which that can be done is to have a report after investigation or survey. At every election this question comes up and we are all in favour of a tunnel, but so far nothing has been done, and the question has caused

a pood deal of agitation, I would not say turmoil, in the province of Prince Edward Island. It has been a burning question there for some years, and I agree with what has been very properly said, that in order that there should be a feeling of good will and peace and harmony among the provinces of Canada, in order to consolidate them, if on no other ground, we are entitled to have this question of the practicability and cost of the tunnel set before our people. If it can be done at a reasonable cost, at such a cost as the province would expect to have expended for that work, then I say we should have it, but it is most important and highly desirable to our people that the question should be settled one way or the other. I cannot complain of the large expenditure made in western Canada because I am well aware that the expenditures made there under a careful administration such as we have are necessary and are for the building up of this great nation of ours. At the same time, our people take the view that while these expenditures are being made in other parts of Canada, we in Prince Edward Island contribute our share to these expenditures, and we are entitled to some consideration in the matter of the construction of public works, and especially in the construction of the tunnel. The survey made there some years ago, so far as it went, was probably of considerable service; hut since that time 1 am informed by engineers who are capable of passing an opinion on such subjects that improved means have been discovered of making surveys of that character. I would, the e-fore, urgently call upon the government to take up this matter seriously. The people of Prince county whom I represent are very deeply interested, because one end of this tunnel would most likely be constructed from Cape Travers in that county. I can assure this honourable House that this is a burning question in that province, and our people are most anxious that some steps should be taken with a view of satisfying the public with regard both to the cost and the practicability of the construction of a tunnel. I feel that we have the sympathy of the members from the other provinces of Canada, especially from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and whatever support we get from them will strengthen the hands of the government in at least ordering a survey. I can only express the hope that at an early date the government will see its way clear to take some steps to have an investigation on the lines I have indicated. It is a work which would do much for Prince Edward Island, the garden of the gulf, and would do much to bring about a better state of feeling among the people because as has been very well said, we are the only province in which there Mr. RICHARDS.
is a feeling of irritation and annoyance. I shall say no more on the present occasion, but I hope before the session is over to have another opportunity of dealing at greater length with this important question.

I wish to endorse what has been so well said by my hon. friend. from Queens, Prince Edward Island (Mr. Warburton), and from Prince, Prince Edward Island (Mr. Richards) on this question. There are no two sides to it in our province, upon this subject at least we are at one. I am sure that seventy-five per cent, perhaps ninety-live per cent of the people of our province desire to have the conditions of confederation carried out if at all possible. One of the conditions under which our province entered into the confederation of this great Dominion, and perhaps the chief condition, was the promise of continuous communication with the mainland. We have that in our bond, and we desire to see it carried out by the Dominion government. If that is a condition that cannot be carried out, then we w'ant to know it as soon as possible. At present it is, as my hon. friends have pointed out, an ever recurring subject of turmoil and trouble at every election, whichever government is in power; I think it is the same with both parties. On the eve of every election certain parties go down there and promise, or half promise, that this tunnel shall be constructed, but when the election is over we hear very little about the tunnel until the next election is coming on. Under these circumstances our people are getting discouraged. We trust now, seeing that we are some distance from an election, that this government will at once undertake to ascertain whether a tunnel can be constructed at a reasonable cost. It has been said that such a tunnel would cost an enormous sum of money, some people have placed it as high as $150,000,000. We will not ask for a tunnel if it costs half that amount. The people of our province do not wish to be unreasonable, we do not ask for any thing unreasonable, we only ask this government to make a proper effort to ascertain what the tunnel is likely to cost. We trust that at this present session the government will set aside a certain sum to have a thorough survey made. We do not want a survey that will be barren of any reliable and useful information, we want a complete survey made, cost what it will, and we want the survey made as soon as possible. This is a question that should not enter into politics, because it is an obligation about which there can be no question. We feel that the federal government should carry out the condition under which we became part of this great Dominion, and that we are entitled to this tunnel. We contribute our full share to the public exchequer, indeed some people argue

that for many years past we have contributed more to the treasury at Ottawa than we are getting back in any shape. It has been figured out pretty closely that we are contributing a larger sum each year, more than we are getting back. Now if that is so, it must be plain that we are entitled to to see this matter taken hold of seriously by the government. Without saying any more at the present on this subject, I have great pleasure in endorsing what has been said by my hon. friends from that province, and I hope that the government will take heed to it and act upon it without delay.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The question that has been brought to the notice of the House by my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. Warburton), my hon. friend from Prince, Prince Edward Island (Mr. Richards), and my hon. friend from Kings, Prince Edward Island (Mr. Fraser), is, I am well aware, of the deepest interest to the people of Prince Edward Island, and they are quite right when they claim that it ought to be regarded as a matter of general interest to the people of the Dominion. It is a good many years since this question was first brought before the House of Commons. Perhaps it would not be too much to say that in the earlier days the matter was regarded by many members as somewhat impracticable, and possibly even visionary; and for a long time it was hardly treated with the seriousness that our friends from Prince Edward Island desired. But I am glad to recognize the fact that the progress of engineering science in recent years has brought into the realm of practical affairs many projects which years ago would have been regarded unfavourably, and I am inclined to think that one of the matters that has been brought within that realm is the question of a Prince Edward Island tunnel. The subject has been brought before the House from time to time, and I must in justice to my hon. friends say that in no case when I have been present, or when I have read the debates, has it been presented better than to-day. It has been presented to-day forcibly, reasonably and with great moderation, and 1 compliment my three hon. friends for presenting the matter in that way. If I have to dissent from anything that has been said, it is in view of the words uttered by the hon. member for Kings who treated this matter as an obligation under the Confederation Act, Frankly I do not agree with my hon. friend.
I do not think that this is an obligation under the Confederation Act. I do not think the government of Canada, either of one party or the other, has failed in its obligation to the people of Prince Edward Island to carry out the conditions of confederation. But though I differ from my hon. friend in that respect, that does not in 10
the slightest degree affect my disposition to sympathize with Prince Edward Island, and to help the people of that province in this matter. I am disposed to think that if it can be had at a moderate cost the people of Prince Edward Island should have this tunnel, not because it is an obligation of confederation, for I humbly think it is not, but because they may fairly ask it in order that they may keep pace with the progress of the times, and that they may receive a share of the benefits of the great growing time in Canada irrespective of whether it is an obligation of eonfedera-ton or not. I look upon Prince Edward Island as one of the fairest provinces of the Dominion. In many respects it is one of the happiest provinces of the Dominion. It is an island almost entirely devoted to agriculture, settled by a fine farming population, by a very intelligent people, and there is no part of the Dominion of Canada, nay, there is probably no part of the world, where the blessings and comforts of life are more evenly distributed than they are among the good people of Prince Edward Island. Nevertheless, the population does not grow. Occasionally, indeed, there are indications that the population is falling away and our island friends are naturally very much disturbed on that account, They think their chief difficulty is this question of transportation. In the past very large figures have been quoted as the probable cost of this work. I am glad to hear my hon. friends from the island say that all they ask is that this matter shall be thoroughly and impartially inquired into and if the tunnel can be built at a moderate cost they think the work should be done. To that' sentiment I most heartily subscribe, and I am quite sure that the government will have that feeling towards it. There have been some surveys in the past. I suppose that each of them in its day served the purpose, it was the best that could be had ; but I quite agree with my hon. friends that the matter should be taken up more vigorously and more seriously, and that we should endeavour to get a reliable and thorough survey by the best engineers, and if, as a result of that survey, it is found that this important work can be constructed at a moderate cost, I for one, would promise my hon. friends from Prince Edward Island my most hearty and cordial support.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. DANIEL (St. John City) moved :
speechtext:
For a copy of all reports, correspondence and other papers relating to the condition and maintenance of the buoy on the Old Proprietor Ledge in the Bay of Fundy since January 1, 1908; also of all reports, correspondence



and other papers relating to the establishment, equipment, maintenance and operation of the life boat and life saving station at Seal Cove in the Bay of Bundy; also copy of all instructions issued to Captain Lugar in connection with the inquiry into the wreck of the ss. ' Hestia,' and of the findings and report on said inquiry.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, in making the
motion which I have just read calling for the papers which' the motion calls for it will be necessary for me, to some extent, to call to the minds of the members of this House the unfortunate and disastrous wreck which took place in the Bay of Fundy on the night of the 24th, or early in the morning of the 25th of October last. The wreck of the steamship 'Hestia' is, as far as my memory goes, the most disastrous wreck, in so far as loss of life is concerned, that has ever taken place in the Bay of Fundy. The crew of the steamship numbered 41, and, in addition, there were four passengers, making 45 in all. Of these 45 persons, 39 went down to a watery grave. The facts given simply and shortly, are these:	On the evening of Sunday, 24th
October, the steamship 'Hestia' rounded into the Bay of Fundy, passing the Lurcher Light about eight o'clock. At half past twelve she sighted the Gannet Rock light and at ten minutes after one in the morning she rushed on to the rocks known as the Old Proprietor reef, passing at that time, in order to get into that position, within 30 or 40 feet of what is known as a gas or whistling buoy erected to guard against that very reef and known as Old Proprietor buoy. We all know that the life of a sailor is at all times a dangerous one, that he constantly takes his life in his hands. He is exposed to the danger of collision in darkness and fog. He is subject to the dangers both of wind and waves, of storms and hurricanes even when he has plenty of sea room on the broad Atlantic or on any other ocean, but as he nears the land and approaches his destination there is no doubt that the anxiety of the navigator increases very greatly, more especially when he approaches the shore at night time or in thick weather. This Sunday evening that I have referred to it was raining, clearing at intervals, with some mist, with a north-easterly wind, bearing to some extent on the starboard bow of the ship and tending to drive her to the westward of her course. The fact that these dangers when approaching the coast are very considerable for the navigator is well known and has long been recognized by all maritime nations. The consequence is that they have and are spending a great deal of money to provide suitable aids to navigation where they are needed in the shape of lighthouses, buoys, fog whistles, whistling buoys, floating buoys and very many other aids that human ingenuity has devised in Mr. DANIEL.
order to point out the right course or as a warning beacon to ward off the ship against the hidden dangers, or dangers of any kind, that may be provided against by a light or such other aid to navigation. The principal aids to navigation are all listed and charted so that all the captains and men responsible for the navigation of vessels may become acquainted with all these lights and aids. When coming into any region they have on their charts a statement of these aids and are able to look for them when they require to do so as their course develops and they go on their path towards their proper haven. If it is necessary, as of course it is, that all these things should be made known and the information placed in the hands of people who ought to have it, the navigators or captains, then surely we will readily understand that it is much more important, that where anything happens to these aids to navigation, when the light goes out, or a buoy goes adrift, that these men who go up and down the great highways of the sea should be made acquainted with all accidents of that nature and with any changes that may be made in the listed lights and buoys around any particular coast.
The course which is generally pursued when anything goes wrong with these lights is, for the Marine Department to notify the British Board of Trade which issues a monthly bulletin to be placed in the hands of navigators so that they may be informed of any changes which take place; and not rely on these lights being in' their accustomed places. In the Bay of Fundy we have such fixed lights as the Gannett rock light, and there are also these automatic gas whistling buoys which are not fixed on lighthouses but which are equally important to the navigator. Such a light was placed on what is known as the Old Proprietor reef. Off the southern coast of Grand Manan there is a very dangerous reef mostly covered by water which on the eastward juts out on the course which is taken by vessels going to St. John and other ports on the bay. This sunken reef at its outermost end raises its gnarled and scarred surface above the water and it is called the Old Proprietor rock, and for years there has. been a high mast on that rock. Some years ago the St. John Board of Trade petitioned the Marine Department to place a lighthouse on that rock, but the request was refused on the ground that the expense would be too great. However, on account of the great danger of this reef the Department of Marine placed, a mile or so to the southward of the rock, one of those automatic whistling buoys supplied by Messrs. Willson, of Ottawa, and which I think cost $8,000. This buoy was for two or three years in commission and was regularly listed and charted. It was one of the most important lights in the Bay of Fundy

and had it been in working order on the. night of October 24, or the morning of October 25, there would not have occurred that disaster by which thirty-nine persons found a watery grave, and among them two little Scotch lads who were coming out to settle in this country. It was most pathetic to read in the account of that wreck that *when these two little lads were overturned in the boat the voice of one of the little ones in his Scotch accent was heard to cry out over the wateis:	Oh, mother,
mother, save me, I am drowning. But these two little boys, together with two other passengers and the thirty-five hardy sailors, including the captain and all of the deck officers, except one, were drawn down in that waste of waters on that night. I say, Sir, and I say it calmly and coolly, that in their death they were the victims of either the inaction or the indifference or the incapacity of the responsible officers of the Marine Department. Had the defect in that buoy been remedied, it would not be in my power nor in the power of any one to point an accusing finger at the Department of Marine. But, Sir, the agent of that department knew as long ago as January the 22nd last, ten months ago, that the light was out or that the buoy was adrift. Now, what action was taken? They put an advertisement in three of the St. John papers and they inserted that advertisement three times and it read:
Tlie Old Proprietor gas and whistling buo.v has been reported as being either adrift or the light out. It will be attended to as soon as possible.
. Signed J.
Jan. 26, 1909.
E. LEGERE, Acting Agent
So far as I know that was the only notice given in printed form, but I understand that the agent of the Donaldson line in St. John was. verbally notified that there was something wrong with the buoy. Now, was that buoy attended to as soon as possible as stated in the advertisement? Is it necessary to take ten months to put right one of these gas buoys? I put a question to the Minister of Marine on the point and the minister allowed himself to be made the mouthpiece of an answer which stated that the weather conditions and press of more important affairs would not allow of that buoy being attended to. But, Sir, only a week after the wreck took place that buoy which for ten months lay there neglected, was towed into St. John harbour and tested opposite Partridge Island. All summer long, for ten months, the weather conditions would not allow the department to put this buoy right, but in the stormy month of November, in less than a week after the wreck they could go out there and tow it into harbour and set it in order.
Why was not the ' Lansdowne ' sent to attend to this, matter? I would like to ask the minister, so that when he speaks on this subject he will be able to say whether there is any regulation in the department to the effect that that steamer should only leave port when it had several jobs to attend to. I understand that the acting agent at St. John, when asked why he did not send the ' Lansdowne ' there, gave that as one of his reasons. I know that day after day and week after week the ' Lansdowne ' was lying in the harbour at St. John, and might easily have been sent during the summer months when the weather was fine. It is ridiculous for the minister to say that the weather conditions were such, in one of the finest summers we ever had, that the steamer was unable to go to that buoy. When I heard the minister give that reply, I was astounded. I do not think that even for the purpose of screening his department,, which he might naturally be expected to desire to do, he should allow such a ridiculous answer to be put into his mouth as that for ten months in the year the weather conditions in the Bay of Fundy were such that a steamer oi the size of the 'Lansdowne' should not go and tow up a buoy of the size of that on the Old Proprietor ledge. The thing to my mind is utterly absurd and farcical. He also says that press of more important business prevented. I would like the minister to say what that more important business was. I would like to call his attention to the fact that that buoy is considered the most important among all the aids to navigation in the whole Bay of Fundy. What did Captain Gillies say on that very point in the investigation which was held? He said:
The neighbourhood of the Grand Manan has always been acknowledged to be the most dangerous locality in the whole hay.
There is the statement of a practical navigator; and yet the minister says that he spent nearly the whole year in looking after more important business while this steamer was lying in the harbour of St. John. To give you some idea of the importance of these aids to navigation in the Bav of Fundv, and the necessity of having them kept in the best possible condition, let me remind the House that in the year 1908-9 there was exported from the city and port of St. John alone for transatlantic ports no less than $24,564,840 worth of goods. I would also like to give the House an idea of the number of vessels trading up and down the bay. I will read from the annual report of the St. John Board of Trade the figures for the last three years 1906, 1907 and 1908, of the arrivals and clearances of the port of St. John:

Besides the tonnage entering and leaving the port of St. John, there is the shipping business of all the bay ports on both the Nova Scotia side and the New Brunswick side. Not that all the vessels take the easterly side of the Grand Manan in going inwards and outwards, but all the large steamers do, and pass this Old Proprietor ledge. This buoy was known for ten months to be defective, and that' fact is entirely responsible for the wreck of the ' Hestia.' In this connection I wish to read letter of the only deck officer whose life was saved after the wreck, that is, the third officer, S. A. Stewart. On the 2nd of November this letter was published in the St. John 'Globe'. It is headed:
Aids to Navigation in Bay of Fundy-Strong
Statement by Third Officer of ss. ' Hestia.'
Seal Cove, Grand Manan, Oct. 31. To the Editor of the 'Globe ':
Sir,-I inclose herewith a letter from the third officer of the stranded steamer ' Hestia,' setting forth his views and expressing his feelings in this matter. We would ask you to publish the letter in your paper as early as convenient to you, as we think it would he of interest to the general public and possibly remedy a great evil.
Unless something is done the insurance rates will certainly increase on Bay of Fundy trade, which will act against St. John, New Brunswick.
WILLIAM H. LOGAN, Salvage Officer, Salvage Association,
London.
M. V. Gillies,
Supt. Donaldson Line.

Stewart, third officer of the ' Hestia,' speaking of the stranding and subsequent happenings of that vessel and her crew, says:
The night we stranded there was a strong northeast wind with thick rainy weather, clearing at intervals, short high sea running. We were steering a mid-channel course up the Mr. DANIEL.
bay, and our frequent soundings of over a hundred fathoms were satisfactory-
About half an hour after midnight on Sunday, October 24, Gannet Rock light was sighted, but owing to weather conditions accurate distance off could not possibly be established. The captain kept the ship on her course, evidently looking for the Old Proprietor buoy. At 1.10 on 25-10-'09, the ship struck on the outer part of the latter named ledge, where when the tide rose she fell over on her side and was completely submerged at high water. Myself, the second engineer and four seamen are all that remain alive out of a crew of 41 men.	_
I find since being brought ashore here that the light keepers in Gannet Rock lighthouse saw the ship passing, also that there is a large whistle and lighted buoy between the Gannet Rook and Old Proprietor shoals. All seamen entering the Bay of Fundy are compelled to depend upon these aids to navigation and if they were not there would not enter the bay under such weather conditions as existed on the night in question.
1 feel, on behalf of myself and my brother officers and the many men who have lost their lives, also in the general interests of shipping trading to Bay of Fundy ports, that a strong protest to the department responsible for the lighthouse and buoyage system should be made through the public press, against the existing conditions of the aids to navigation on this dangerous coast.
My direct complaint is that the Old Proprietor Ledge buoy has heither light nor fog signal, whereas it is listed as having both. It is also well known locally that this buoy has been in this condition for months; while it is known that the ' Hestia ' must have passed within a few feet of this buoy it will readily be conceded that had it been lit or its whistle sounding the ship would have been warned and cleared easily the ledges upon which she was wrecked. Doubtless the captain, after seeing the Gannet, was looking for this buoy. Can any one imagine a worse trap laid for any man than a buoy listed as marking dangerous ledges, and having a light working at stated intervals, also an automatic whistle signal, whilst neither whistle nor light exist? It is simply a trap worse than any ever thought of by even the old time wreckers that are now but a winter's tale. It is impossible to describe one's feelings when he finds that what he thought was his great factor of safety has proved his ruin.
In the bitterness with which one looks upon the dreadful loss of life that certainly would not have been if those responsible for the conditions of the Old Proprietor Ledge buoy had attended to their ordinary everyday duties; for there is not a shadow of a doubt the loss of the ' Hestia ' is due to the long neglected conditions of this buoy.
Again, the keeper of the Gannet admits he did not fire a warning gun because he was afraid he might awake the doctor. Can anyone imagine a man, keeper of an outlying lighthouse, seeing a vessel standing into a probable danger, and not warning her because he thought the doctor misrht mistake the signal as being intended for him. A few explosive signals from the lighthouse would have been quite sufficient to warn this ship and

save her from destruction; still they were not given, although the keeper admits seeing the vessel and thinking her too close in, because they might call the doctor; and the vessel was allowed to go to her end. Is there any way of describing such stupidity or incompetence? Will the Canadian people allow such things to be? Let them try to think what it would mean if this accident had happened to one of the large passenger vessels plying to St. John, particularly when it is known that there is no life-saving station in the neighbourhood. There is supposed to be one, but it now consists of a boat unfit for use and without a crew. We were from 1.10 a.m. on Monday until noon Tuesday in a helpless and perilous position before any one came near the ship. Notwithstanding our being but four miles from the Gannet Rock lighthouse and making distress signals night and day; especially Monday night, which was clear and fine with all shore lights plainly visible, and during which bonfires were burnt on board the wreck almost continuously.
I would pray that the people of Canada may insist that those who are responsible for the coast lighting and buoyage system will keep that system in order or not put buoys out at all, so that there may not be traps added to a profession which already bristles with difficulty and much danger.

Third Officer ss. ' Hestia.'
Seal Cove, October 81, 1909.
That is the statement of the only surviving deck officer of the steamship ' Hestia.' With regard to the conditions of this light, let me refer to the evidence taken at the investigation. Here is the evidence of the first witness, Oolin MacVicar, able seaman. In reply to a question put by Mr. Boyer, who was counsel for the department, he said:
That he had seen the Old Proprietor buoy from the ship as she lay on the rocks on Monday morning, but heard no whistle from the buoy nor was any light visible thereon Monday night.
The next witness was Andrew West Morgan, second engineer of the wrecked vessel, who was saved. He said:
During both Monday and Tuesday the .buoy on the Old Proprietor reef was plainly visible during the daytime about a mile away, but he heard no whistle from it, nor was there any light upon it at night.
The next evidence I will give is that of the gentleman whose letter I have just read, the third officer :
The witness was of the opinion that the captain expected and hoped to take up the Old Proprietor buoy. Had the light on the buoy been burning, the accident could not have happened, since they must have passed within a few feet of the buoy.
That is the evidence of the third officer.
Mr. Holden, continuing the examination of Stewart, asked him whether, in his opinion as
a navigator, the ship would have gone on the rocks had the Old Proprietor buoy light been burning to which Stewart gave a decided negative.
Mr. Holden went on to ask him this question:
I will ask the witness whether the fact that the light supposed to be on the Old Proprietor buoy has been non-existent during the whole summer, has been officially brought to the notice of mariners.
The answer is:
Never in any form.
Then there is the evidence of Captain Gillies with regard to the neighbourhood of Grand Manan being the most dangerous in the whole locality. There is no need of citing more evidence of that nature; it is all of the same kind and it must be of the same kind because it cannot be denied.
One would suppose that under these circumstances, when it was shown that this buoy had not been lit or its whistle sounding, and that this had been known for almost a year, a strict investigation would be held into the matter. You would also suppose that there would he some investigation into the cause of a wreck in which 39 lives were lost and an attempt made to ascertain whether all was done that should have been done to put that buoy and keep that buoy in its proper position and every possible effort made to succour the survivors. But what was the result? We have had a so-called investigation but, Sir, an investigation that was incomplete and literally farcical in its denouement. From all that I can learn Captain Lugar, who was chairman of the commission, stated on the streets of St. John before he had taken a particle of evidence that the cause of this vessel going on the rocks was because the compasses were deviating on account of her cargo of iron. According to the press, orders were given that there should be held a secret inquiry into this most disastrous wreck. I believe there was some secret inquiry but that did not by any means commend itself to the common sense or the ordinary judgment of the people down there and there was an immediate agitation for a public inquiry. Then it was stated there would be a public inquiry. It would be expected that the public inquiry would be held in the port of St. John where every available witness was -at hand to be subpoenaed. But what was done? Suddenly we were told that the inquiry was to be removed to Montreal. Why? It was stated that the survivors were there. As a matter of fact the survivors were not there. The survivors were taken there after it was given out that the inquiry was tb be held there. Then it was stated that Montreal was more central.

More central to what? To the centre of Canada. Then why not take it out at once to the city of Winnipeg? When you take it to Montreal you are taking it away from the men who were in the ship, from the pilots who would be able to give information and from the keeper of the lighthouse, from those who had gone down in tug boats to the wreck and rendered what assistance they could, from every one who was there ready to give his testimony. What was the resuit? Why Sir, I think with all honesty that we can only come to the conclusion that this so called investigation was not intended to investigate, it was intended more to screen the officials of the department responsible for the condition of this buoy. Otherwise it would appear to me and I think to every reasonable man that an investigation intended to be thorough, intended to be what it was called, would have been held right down there in the midst of those who were in a position to give true and honest testimony, and in the nearest place to the scene of the wreck. There were the survivors, the representatives of the steamship company, the pilots, those who had been off to the ship, the lighthouse keeper, and all of them were there ready to testify and easily accessible. But the inquiry was removed to Montreal. What was the result? We get a finding such as one would have expected, if the statement I have made with regard to Captain Lugar before the investigation was correct and I believe it was. The finding reads:
The court is of the opinion that the cause which led to the foundering of the steamship ' Hestia ' on the Old Proprietor ledge were An error in the compass, due probably to what is known as Gauss's error, aided probably by the fact that the vessel carried a cargo of 800 tons of iron.
The statement he made before he held any investigation at all, whereas the evidence in that investigation did not give Captain Lugar the slightest reason for saying that there was any error in the compass of that ship. All the evidence I have seen, and of course I have only seen the evidence reported in the newspapers, is to the effect that the compasses were all right and that before that ship left Glasgow she was swung, the compass was tested and the deviation was found to be extremely slight. What other evidence have we that the compasses were true? Why Sir, the very fact that that ship sailed from Glasgow to the mouth of the Bay of Fundy on her direct course, without any going to the right or left. If her compasses had been wrong, would the ship have made the mouth of the Bav of Fundy just as she expected to do and at the time she expected to get there? That fact of itself is enough to show that the compasses were in proper order and it is supported by the evidence of the surviving officer that the ship was swung in Glas-Mr. DANIEL.
gow after her cargo had been placed On board and her compasses were found true. That is enough to show that the finding was not warranted by the evidence or by the facts.
I want to say this: Supposing the compasses were out of order, there is no doubt the vesesel was off her course. Is that any excuse why the light and the whistle of the Old Proprietor buoy should be out of order after having been ten months in that condition? What is the need of a buoy on the Old Proprietor, or anywhere else, if a vessel is in her course and everything is going well and right? These aids to navigation are wanted when things go wrong, and not when they go right. I have called attention to the fact that this board has stated that the compasses were wrong. Secondly, it says :
The neglect of the master to take soundings when in sight of the Gannet rock. .
3.	Allowance was not made for the tides and the set of the wind.
4.	An error of judgment on the part of the master in allowing his ship to get the bearing of the Gannet Kock light to southwest of west nagnetic. It must be borne in mind that the ship was only five and a half miles from Gan-net rock when she struck.
Now, Sir, there are the facts as I have learned them from the finding, and I think I have shown the common sense and judgment of this House that that finding was not borne out either by the evidence or by the facts.
The other point I wish to bring before the House is that in that finding no mention whatever is made of the fact that the Old Proprietor buoy light was out, and that the whistle was not sounding. Now, what sort of an investigation is that? Here you set out to find the cause of the wreck, and the actual and veritable cause of the wreck is not mentioned at all. It was utterly impossible for that vessel to have gone on the Old Proprietor rock if that buoy had been lighted or the whistle sounding. It is idle to say that the ship's compasses were out, or that the master had not been making his soundings as he ought to have done, or that other things had happened, when, if the one requisite thing had been done, the wreck would never have taken place. If the man, or men, or officials, responsible for the proper condition of that light had attended to their duty, these 39 people, little boys and grown up men, would now be enjoying life with the rest of us, instead of being buried under the waters of the Bay of Fundy. That is the charge which this wreck, this unnecessary wreck, brings against the Department of Marine and Fisheries. -
Another point I wish to bring out is that the commissioners state that these other things would be the subject of a later inquiry, that is, with regard to the buoy, and

with regard to the coolness of the lighthouse keeper and other matters of that kind, and I hope that when the minister gets up to speak he will be able to give a satisfactory assurance to this House and the country on those points. I can assure him that the greatest interest is taken in this matter, more especially by those who are interested in the ownership and in the sailing and operation of ships, and by those who aTe interested in the maritime affairs of this country, and in the proper operation of the buoy system, and the system of marine aids generally upon which we have been spending so much money for many years past. To these people this is a most vital question. I do not think the people will be Dut off with any such farcical so called investigation as we have been treated to so far, but will insist, and I hope will obtain, a proper and serious investigation into all these matters. Why, Sir, if a man lost his life through violence on land, there would be an inquest held, and some attempt would be made to find out how he came to his; death, who was responsible for it. But here are 39 lives wiped out within an hour or two, and no attempt is made to ascertain why all these people were drowned, and why only six were saved out of the whole number of crew and passengers. I hope the minister will explain these matters, because I can assure him that the people of the maritime provinces are losing confidence in the department over which he has the honour to preside. It will not do for him to allow any want of confidence in that department to exist, more especially in regard to the operation of aids to navigation, and the buoyage system on that extensive coast, and indeed on both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts. I hope he will be able to satisfy this parliament and this country that he intends to have this matter properly investigated, and whatever is wrong, to have it righted. With regard to the acting agent of marine at St. John, who appears to be the responsible party, I have nothing to say, I have never met him, I do not know him. The only facts I know are those that I have been trying to present this afternoon. But I do not mind saying this, Mr. Speaker, that if Mr. Fred Harding had been retained in his position as agent of that department, and in the post from which he was removed, so far as I can see, without proper cause, the department at Ottawa would not have remained for ten months without being made acquainted with the condition of that Old Proprietor buoy, nor would that Old Proprietor buoy have been allowed to remain ten months in that condition without being remedied.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I may say that there is certainly no objection to the motion which has been made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Daniel) being adopted. I will be very glad indeed to bring down all the papers concerning this unfortunate accident to the ' Hestia,' and at the same time the papers concerning the establishment of the life-saving station on Seal Cove. I do not think there were any special instructions given to Capt. Lugar, but I will bring down all the instructions special instructions given to Capt. Lugar, which may have been given to him of a general character.
And the different instructions which, I understand, he received-instructions fox a secret inquiry in the. first place and after that a public inquiry in St. John and later in Montreal?

Certainly, I shall be very glad and besides I will say a word or two later on in my remarks in regard to that phase of the question. I may say that I am very glad that my hon. friend has given me an opportunity of putting before the public the side of the department in regard to this question.. I do not want to find any fault at all with my hon. friend for having brought the discussion before the House, because I know that this matter has received the attention of the public especially in St. John and in his province, and I suppose that he felt it was his duty to bring the matter before the country. Generally speaking, I am not much in favour of having these questions of wrecks discussed publicly in the press or before parliament and I will tell my hon. friend why. There has been in late years very serious discrimination by the insurance men against our Canadian ports, so much so, that to-day there is great difference between the insurance rates charged for a vessel going to Portland and for a vessel going to St. John, or Halifax, or to the St. Lawrence. There might be some reason for this discrimination with regard to the St. Lawrence because vessels have to navigate a long stretch of water and it might be found that accidents occur more frequently than in the ports of New York, Boston or Portland. But, in view of the improvements that we have made, in view of the aids to navigation we have established in the St. Lawrence, I think I may affirm now that, the accidents that occur in that part of the country are very much less in number than those that happen on some other routes where shipping is carried on to the same extent. But, though I deprecate the discussion of these accidents, because they

become too prominent sometimes before the public and because they justify, to a certain extent, the underwriters charging higher rates, I feel that in this case my hon. friend was perfectly justified, in view of the discussion which has taken place in his province and especially in his own city, in bringing the matter before the public.
As far as the department is concerned, I am also very glad to have the occasion of discussing this question because I think I may say to my hon. friend and the House that the rumours that have been set in motion, the charges which in some cases have been made of negligence on the part of the officials, are charges that cannot be substantiated. The officer who was largely responsible for carrying out the work in the St. John district is Mr. Legere, who was acting agent at the time. Mr. Legere is certainly a very good officer. He was assistant engineer in the department under Col.'Anderson and I must bear testimony to his character as an officer. I think I cannot do better than quote what is to be found in the last report of Col. Anderson, in which he states:
Tile assistant engineers appointed to attend to details of construction in the several outlying portions of the Dominion have rendered me valuable assistance and I wish again to bear testimony to the efficient work done by Mr. Legere in the maritime provinces.
Mr. Legere is supposed to be one of our best officers. He has been acting assistant engineer for some time and has given entire satisfaction. When last year, on the report of the persons who were making inquiries into the department, I had to take action and suspend the agent in St. John, we looked around and we thought the man who was best qualified to take the place temporarily -was certainly Mr. Legere and he was appointed in St. John as acting agent. My hon. friend has attached a great deal of importance to the gas buoy on Old Proprietor ledge not being lit when the accident happened in the month of October last. I may say that it is not customary for mariners or navigators to rely upon those gas buoys; in fact, if, in a place like the Bay of Fundy, or south of Nova Scotia, you rely entirely, or to a large extent, upon the gas buoys which are there, you will find it is very difficult because one of the greatest problems that we have to deal with in the department is to keep these buoys in proper order. I will take the opportunity later on to read part of a report made by Mr. Legere concerning the work which he has done there since January last and it will be seen from that report how difficult it is to keep these buoys in proper condition. It is no wonder. The tide is very high, the winds aTe sometimes very strong, and the conditions are such that it is very difficult to maintain these buoys in proper Mr. BEODETTR
condition. This is true not only of these buoys but of the buoys that we have as aids to navigation in different parts of the country. In our list of lights and fog signals issued on the first of April, 1909-and the same will be found in previous reports -we have this notice:
Mariners must bear in mind the fact that gas buoys are unwatched and if extinguished some time may elapse before a tender can reach them to repair or relight. Their lights cannot therefore be depended upon in the same way as those shown from watched light lighthouses.
. (Sgd.) G. J. DESBARATS, Acting Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
Not, only in Canada, but in every country in the world and especially in Great Britain, mariners are warned against relying too much not only upon gas buoys, but also upon light houses because accidents may happen to them. In our case we ought not to be too greatly blamed, because in Canada the government of the country renders the light service gratuitously, whereas in England no vessel can enter a harbour without being taxed light dues for the light in that harbour. Now, here is a company which has taken us to task-I should not say the company because I have had no serious complaint from the company-but here is an agent taking us to task who is probably himself largely responsible for the accident that has occurred. Let us see whether the department should be held responsible. I shall give the result of the investigations which have been held later, but I may say now that I regret to find that the agent of the company is trying to put upon the department the responsibility for this accident. The Donaldson line itself has not made any representations to us in that respect; their agents in Montreal have never made any complaint, but on the contrary the correspondence will show that the work we have done has received their appreciation. There is one thing to which I must call the attention of the House and of the public, and it is: We are providing aids to navigation, we are building lighthouses, we are putting in gas buoys, spar buoys, fog alarms, wireless telegraph stations, and equipping in every way, shape, and form, our navigation system on the Pacific and Atlantic coasts. But we must expect that those engaged in the shipping business shall take the necessary steps to utilize the aids to navigation which we supply. In this case, just a few miles from where the accident happened and where such loss of life occurred there is a wireless station-I join in the sympathy my hon. friend has expressed for that loss of life; I am sorry for it, and perhaps more sorry than he is-but I say that if the company had put a wireless telegraph apparatus on their steamer so that they could communi-

cate with the wireless apparatus which we are maintaining at Partridge Island and other places in the locality, the loss of life would not have occurred. Even if the vessel had struck on the rocks she could have communicated with our station at Partridge Island and we could have sent vessels immediately to their assistance. Therefore I say that if the company or its agent find fault with us, I think they are also at fault for not having equipped their vessel with a wireless system. The question is engaging the attention of the American authorities and of the British authorities now, and it should also engage our attention in this parliament, as to whether the steamship companies which are plying to our ports should not be bound to establish a wireless system on their vessels so that loss of life would be prevented, as it would in this case had the steamer been so equipped. Now, the agent of this company at St. John seems to have started an agitation over this accident. Let me say that the agent or his office in St. John was notified that this light was out and I presume he failed to communicate it to the owners of the ' Hes-tia ' or to the master of that ship. There is no evidence to that effect that I know of, but at all events the 'Hestia' was in St. John several times since that notification and the agent should have notified her master that the light was out. I do not know whether he has done so or not. But not only did we notify the agency of the company at St. John, but our acting agent also thought well to publish in the newspapers the following notice which I do not remember that my hon. friend (Mr. Daniel) read.
* Mr. DANIEL. I read the advertisement.

The advertisement was published on the 25th of January, 1909 in the newspapers of St. John, Yarmouth and St. Andrews, and it read as follows:
St. John, N.B., January 25, 1909.
Notice to Mariners:-The old Proprietor gas and whistling buoy has been reported either adrift or light out. It will he attended to as soon as possible.
(Sgd.) J. A. LEGERE, Acting agent, Department of Marine and Fisheries, St. John, N.B.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the first question we have to discuss is what has been the cause of the accident. My hon. friend (Mr. Daniel) says the department is entirely responsible for the accident and he lavs the entire blame on the negligence of the department. I must take issue with my hon. friend in that regard. Before condemning the department, as he has done, I think he should have waited until the papers were brought down. From them he would have found that the accident was not due in any shape or form to the negligence of the
department or of the acting agent at St. John. How did the accident occur? An investigation has taken place. The result of that investigation will be placed before the House, when it will be found, that the accident was in part due to what is called Gaus-sin's error. On that point I might mention the evidence given by one of the survivors of that unfortunate accident, Mr. John Mackenzie. He stated that he was an able seaman to the ss. ' Hestia,' but had lost all his papers. He had been at sea 16 years, 13 of which he had served as an able seaman. It was his first voyage on this ship. She left Glasgow on October 10, and she stranded about ten minutes past one on Monday, October 25. He was at the wheel from 6 to 8 p.m. the previous day. Could not remember the course he steered by the compass; it was given in degrees.
He considered the 'Hestia' was a very bad vessel to steer. She would sheer some times more than a point off her course.
Some of his friends who had made the previous voyage in her advised him strongly not to go because she steered so badly. Here is a man who was on the ship and who makes that extraordinary statement. But, Mr. Speaker, I will not rely entirely on the evidence of that man. I will take the chart itself, and will show to the House that the accident was entirely due to the causes mentioned in the judgment rendered by the commissioner, Capt. Lugar, and the two assessors, Capt. Francis Nash and Capt. Richard Jones, men of a great deal of experience in marine matters. The first cause assigned for the accident is what is called Gauss's error. This, I may say, is an error that ocurs in the following circumstances. When a ship has been for several days on a course, let us say an easterly or westerly course, the soft iron of which the ship is constructed becomes magnetized. The ship in fact becomes a large magnet. In this instance the magnetism of the ship was increased by the fact that she had 800 tons of iron on board. This magnetism does not affect the needle of the compass while the same course is continued, that is, so long as she goes from east to west, from west to east, from north to south, or from south to north. But if at the end of several days the ship's course is changed, as happened in this case, the magnetism of the ship tends to draw the needle to the position in which the ship had been during the previous course. There are two ways in which this error can be remedied-taking the bearings or making soundings. In this case we have no evidence to show whether on the southern coast of Nova Scotia the bearings could be taken or not; but the soundings could have been taken. The soundings appear to have been taken. Now, the chart in my hand shows first that the boat should go from east to west until it reaches Seal Island, where we have a light-

house or a lightship. It should then go in a northwesterly direction until it comes nearly opposite Yarmouth, when it should go straight north in order to pass the Lurcher lightship, when it reaches a point where there' are fifty fathoms of water. Then it should take a straight course to St. John between Gannet rock on the west and Brier Island on the east. We have there two lights, the Brier Island light and the Gannet Rock light. The latter is _ of the second order, that is to say, the third best class of light in the world. I may say that the best class of light in the world is to be found at Cape Race in Newfoundland, a light which has been erected by the Marine Department here. The first order light is similar to one on Sambro near the entrance to Halifax harbour, and the second order light is the one erected at Gannet rock. By the chart of the Admiralty, the vessel, on leaving the Lurcher lightship, should go nearer to Brier Island than to Gannet rock. There is a great distance between the two, but the two lignts can easily be seen. What happened in this case? The captain did not follow this course but evidently got out of his course. If he had been in his right course, and had taken soundings, he would have found a depth of 100 fathoms or more. He went near to Gannet Rock, and instead of directing, his ship towards the northeast, he let her go towards the northwest, and in a few hours she was on the Old Proprietor ledge. The commissioners have taken the evidence, and they conclude as follows in the report signed by Capt. Lugar and the two assessors. With regard to Capt. Lugar, he is certainly one of the most experienced navigators in the country. He has a certificate of the British Board of. Trade, and my hon. friend knows well that the British Board of Trade never gives a certificate except when they know that the man to whom they give it is capable of doing the work. That court decided as follows:
This court is of opinion that the causes which led up to the loss of the ss. 'Hestia,' on October 25, 1909, on Old Proprietor ledge, were as follows:-
1.	Error of compass due probably to Gauss's
error. This vessel had in as cargo about 800 tons of iron.	.
2.	Neglect of soundings when in sight of Gannet Rock light.
There are places, where this vessel was supposed to go, where there are'100 fathoms of water. If the captain had taken proper soundings in approaching Gannet Light, he would have found that there were in some places there only eighteen fathoms, ten fathoms, forty-five fathoms and forty-three fathoms of water. Why did he not change his course instead of continuing west? Was that because, as a witness said, Mr. BRODETJR
the vessel steered badly? Why should the department be held responsible for that?
3.	Not sufficient allowance made for set of ebb tide and strong wind.
The wind was coming from the north east and was supposed to bring the steamer on the Grand Manan and the ledges surrounding. What did the master do? Instead of directing his course north-east just in front of the wind, he went on the other side and came on the rocks.
4.	Error of judgment on the part of the master in allowing ship to get the bearing of Gannet Rock light to the southward of west magnetic. It must he borne in mind the ship was about 5J miles from Gannet light when she stranded.
That is a term absolutely nautical which I shall not undertake to discuss. The ship was about five miles from the Gannet light when she stranded. Here is the decision given by three men, one having a certificate of the British Board of Trade, and the two others being master mariners, and they say the accident was due to the causes I have just mentioned. My hon. friend has said that a secret investigation was held. If he will look over, the Shipping Act he will find that there are two kinds of investigations-the preliminary investigation and the formal investigation. The preliminary investigation is held in private. It is not necessary that the commissioner should act as a court. He simply goes around collecting information and then reports to the minister and advises whether an investigation should be held in full court or not. Capt. Lugar is our wreck commissioner for the maritime provinces, and his instructions are, whenever an accident occurs, to investigate the facts immediately and find out whether a formal investigation should be held or not. A formal investigation is held in order to give a hearing to any of the parties implicated because nobody, under the British constitution, can be convicted without being heard. If it be found at the preliminary inquiry that the captain of the vessel is responsible or other persons on the vessel, a formal investigation is held, but in this case the master unfortunately was lost. There was so much talk however about the accident that I thought it advisable to order a formal investigation in order that the public should be made aware exactly of what happened.
My hon. friend called the first investigation a secret one. That is not what it is called in the Shipping Act. It is called a preliminary investigation and is for the purpose of discovery. My hon. friend goes further. He asks: Why did you hold the investigation in Montreal? Well, the accident happened on the 25th of October. On the 27th, we were notified. My hon. friend will find in the papers, when they come down, that immediately on representations being made by the agents of the vessel, we

ordered two government steamers to go to the rescue-the ' Curlew ' and the ' Lands-downe I received thanks from the agents for this assistance.
