Immediately Captain Lugar left under special instructions for Yarmouth to attend the coroner's investigation, and he reported to us on the 5th of November. He held his preliminary inquiry on the 2nd and 3rd of November. We did not lose any time. He examined all the witnesses who could give information at St. John, and of course he heard the survivors of the accident. Immediately he made his report. On the 4th of November we got the following request from Robert Reford & Company, agents of the Donaldson Line:
Captain Lugar intends holding informal investigation, 10 a.m. Friday, into loss of ss. ' Hestia.' Can we have representation at that inquiry? If our request is not in order, could you arrange hold full, formal investigation while crew are here. Reply wire.
On the 5th of November I appointed Captain Lugar as wreck commissioner in the following words:
Ottawa, Nov. 5, 1909.
I, the honourable Louis Philippe Brodeur, Minister of Marine and Fisheries, by virtue of the powers vested in me under section 781 of the Canadian Shipping Act, chapter 113, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, and amending acts, hereby appoint you a commissioner to hold a formal investigation into the causes which led to the grounding of the ss. ' Hestia ' on the 25th October, 1909, at Old Proprietor ledge, Grand Manan, New Brunswick.	-

On the same day we received from Capt. Lugar, at St. John, a telegram stating that the crew were leaving for Montreal. His message read:
St. John, N.B., Nov. 5, 1909.
Yonr wire with authority from minister too late to stop crew leaving for Montreal. Before holding formal inquiry suggest wait my preliminary report. Hold crew of six survivors in Montreal. The Donaldsons' superintendent wants this formal investigation to be b'g thing; want their lawyer attend and call outside evidence.

When we were informed on November.5 that these men were coming to Montreal we gave instructions immediately to Captain Lugar to proceed to Montreal. We were afraid that the members of the crew would leave Montreal early the next week for the other side, we wanted the investigation to be absolutely complete and what did we do? We simply gave instructions to have the investigation held in Montreal in order that these men might be at our disposal. In fact they were sent to Montreal and were examined there so that the reason assigned by my hon. friend (Mr. Daniel) for not holding the investigation in St. John falls to the ground.
My. hon. friend has stated that at one time a request was made to us for the erection of a lighthouse station at the Old Proprietor ledge and that the department decided not to build it because it would be too expensive. I do not know whether the last statement is absolutely correct, as I have not been able to ascertain the facts since my hon. friend made that statement, but I may say with the knowledge I have of lighthouses of the same kind that it would cost about $150,000 or perhaps $200,000 to build a lighthouse at that place. Besides that what would be the use of such a lighthouse there? The Gannet Rock light,
I understand, is not more than four or five miles from this spot. Some years ago when our lights were of an inferior character a request for such a light would have had more force but now that we have lights like the Gannet Rock light that can be seen for 15 miles, what would be the use of putting another light four or five miles from there? It would be absolutely useless to spend $200,000 for that purpose and I would call my hon. friend's attention to this fact; I am sure he will agree with me that such an expenditure would not be justified under the circumstances. However, I shall inquire into the statement he made, I shall have my officers make a report and if it is found that the erection of a light there might prevent wrecks I will be very glad to favourably consider the erection of a light.
My hon. friend stated also that he heard that the 'Lansdowne' is sent only when there are several matters to attend to. I may say he is entirely mistaken in that respect. As soon as it is reported to the agency of the department that something is wrong with any of our buoys or lighthouses, he has instructions to attend to it immediately and the 'Lansdowne' is supposed to go at once.'
I did not make the statement. I stated that it was reported that the agent had made that statement and given it as an excuse, as one reason why the 'Lansdowne' was not sent to repair this buoy.

That is certainly not the report that was before the department. Our report says that the agent has done his best to have the ship go there to attend to that light.
My hon. friend has also stated that the Gannet Rock light keeper did not show any sign of distress because he was afraid to disturb the doctor who was on shore. I do not know where my hon. friend (Mr. Daniel) got that statement but I have the evidence before me and it appears that the Gannet Rock light keeper never knew of the accident, did not see the vessel passing there. Here is the report of Captain Lugar:

Gannet Rook did not see steamer passing_ or wreck till nearly 30 hours after the stranding on account of rain and fog.
By that statement we see that the charge against the Gannet Rock lightkeeper that he did not warn that vessel falls to the ground.
The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Daniel) says that the department has put in my mouth some statements which on their face are ridiculous. It appears that they declared the other day that pressure of more important business prevented their attending to the buoy at Old Proprietor ledge and my hon. friend went on to say that the port of St. John occupies a very important position. that a large amount of business was carried on through that port and that it is ridiculous for me to state that pressure of more important business prevented attending to that buoy and he intimated that I had stated that St. John was not an important port. My hon. friend may be sure that I realize that the port of St. John is certainly one of the most important ports that we have in^ this country. I am well aware that this port in the winter has been doing a very large amount of business, and it would be certainly a mistake on my part to say anything disparaging as to the importance of that harbour. Not only I but the department realize the importance of the port of St. John. We have done a great deal to improve the service there and my hon. friend has only to look at the chart issued by the Admiralty to find out what we have been doing there in the way of aids to navigation. If my hon. friend goes back only ten years he will not find in the harbour of St. John one half the aids to navigation we are giving there to-day. He will not find any of those gas buoys or the improved lights at Partridge Island, Gannet Rock, Brier Island, the Lurcher Lightship or Seal Island. So it would be very unfair to me to state that I did not realize the importance of the harbour of St. John and I suppose my hon. friend did not intend to put that in my mouth. What the acting agent at St. John stated was that although he was willing and anxious to see that this Old Proprietor ledge buoy was lit, his services were required on more important business, as I shall explain immediately to my hon. friend.
The gas buoy at Old Proprietor ledge is very near the Gannet rock light. There are on the other side of the channel where vessels pass places called the Northwest ledge and the Southwest ledge, and the Yarmouth Fairway buoy. These are places where vessels are passing continually. What occurred ? When instructions were given to the 'Lansdowne ' to go up there and light that buoy, it was found that the buoys at these ledges had gone adrift. My hon. friend will realize im-Mr. BRODEUR.
mediately how dangerous it is to leave buoys adrift on the sea in that region, because if you leave them adrift, and a navigator understood them to be in the proper place, a grave accident might occur. There was on one side of the channel, and on the other side a buoy which was not lighted. So there was no particular danger as to that buoy. But there were on the other side of the channel other buoys which were lighted and which were adrift, and if those buoys were not attended to there might be serious consequences to the trade in that section of the country. Then what did the acting agent do? I think it is due to that gentleman who has been devoting himself so faithfully to his business, to read his report on that matter. It is rather _ long, but since he has been attacked I think it is only fair that his report should be laid immediately before parliament before this discussion ends. My hon. friend will see by it the difficulty ' with which this government had to contend, and the serious situation in which he was placed. Most of those buoys were adrift. There had been during a considerable portion of the year very heavy winds and gales blowing at that place, and when the buoys went adrift it became absolutely necessary for him to look, not only after the Old Proprietor buoy, but also after the others. My hon. friend will also see in that report that he tried several times to reach the Old Proprietor buoy during a period of four months, and the gales were so heavy that he found it impossible to reach it and relight it. This was a very serious situation, and I cannot understand why, in face of the difficulties which those officers had to encounter, in face of the duties which those captains had to perform in keeping these aids to navigation in proper shape, we should insult them by charging them with dereliction of duty. I will read that report. It is dated November 6, 1909:
1 beg to submit the following report in answer to yonr telegram of October 30, 1909.
The light on the Old Proprietor gas buoy was reported out, or gone adrift by the keeper of Gull Cove light, January 22, 1909. On January 23 I ordered the ' Lansdowne * to sea, and am inclosing a copy of my letter to tbo captain. You will note at the time the Old Proprietor was reported out that the Yarmouth Fairway was adrift.
My hon. friend knows what the Yarmouth Fairway buoy is.
The agent at Halifax, Mr. Parsons, having wired me as follows, on January 21, 1909.
' Cacouna ' reported Yarmouth Fairway adrift 19th, 10 miles W.S.W. Seal island. We marconied ' Lady Laurier ' ' Shelburne ' rescue. If possible you place another buoy Fairway, we bringing buoy Halifax. Inform board of trade.

My hon. friend will admit that the Yarmouth Fairway waa a very important buoy, more important than the others.
Does the minister mean the Board of Trade there?

I do not know whether it is the Board of Trade there or the Board of Trade of a Canadian city, but I suppose it is the British Board of Trade. Then he goes on:	.
You will note that I arranged to send a Trinity bell buoy to replace the one adrift at Yarmouth Fairway.
In the meantime the Southwest ledge, Brier Island, buoy was reported adrift on January 23, 1909, by the signal agent at Westport, N.S., an in his telegram he stated* ss. ' Westport ' had gone out to tow it in, but later he advised me that the steamer had returned without the buoy.
On January 27, Capt.'Bissett wired that the Old Proprietor was in position,-
Capt. Bissett was the captain of the * Lansdowne.'
-but the sea was too heavy to light lamp, stated no word of South West ledge buoy yet- strong gales and heavy sea. Search was maintained, and on January 30, the South West Ledge buoy was located, one moori HL' stone gone. On Friday 3, Capt. Bissett wired that the South West ledge had been placed in position.
My hon. friend knows what the North West ledge is; That is a very dangerous place near Brier Island. Vessels, according to the information I have in my hands, are passing there, and if that buoy had been adrift or nearer the shore, some vessels might have come to grief. It was more necessary to look after that buoy.
Is that a light buoy?

Yes, the North West ledge and the South West ledge are two light buoys.
The North West ledge had been reported out, some time during the latter end of December, 1908, and an effort was now made to nave this buoy attended to. On February 5, Capt. Bissett wired that he had placed the hel1 buoy at the North West ledge, but could not take up the gas buoy.
In the meantime, on February 2, I received telegrams from Mr. Tremaine of Halifax, stati,ng that the Yarmouth (S.W.) Fairway automatic gas buoy was still at Abbott's Harbour, having been towed there by the ' Ralph.' E. S.' on January 22. This buoy had been reported to the Halifax agency.
On Friday 6, when I saw poor progress at North West ledge, I wired Capt. Bissett, stating he had better proceed to Abbott's harbour and to attend the South West Yarmouth and do the North West ledge on the way hack; also wired him on February 3, as follows:- ' When through with Brier Island, proceed to Abbott's Harbour and if gas buoy Yarmouth (S.W.) Fairway not damaged and can be
moored in position, do so. Also upright Can-dlebox and another upturned buoy whose name you may find locally.
On February 6, I received a telegram from the caotain stating he had just returned from the North West Brier Island gas buoy, with no chance to take hold of it. Asked if he should wait and finish there, or proceed to Abbott's Harbour.
On February 8, I received a further telegram from the captain at Westport, stating that he had been out tp the North West Ledge buoy, but that it was blowing hard from the northeast and he could not get near it owing to heavy sea. He also stated the buoy to he one mile west of true position, and that on the previous day the chances looked favourable for this day, also advised he would proceed to Abbott's Harbour first chance, and that he had only 25 tons of coal in bunkers.
On February 8, Messrs Hugh Cann & Sons, of Yarmouth, N.S., wired me that the Yarmouth North West automatic gas buoy found adrift had been towed to Yarmouth by their boat.
My hon. friend, I suppose, would not deny that this part of the bay is very important too, because there are vessels running every day, if not every day, several times a week, between Yarmouth and Boston, and it is of the utmost importance for the coasting trade that these buoys should be kept in proper position.
On the 10th of February, I received a telegram from Capt. Bissett, as follows:-Arrived here last evening, got buoys alongside and moorings on board, wire in had condition, chain fair, stones gone. Reported here that buoy at Abbott's Harbour is South West gas ' Fairway. Want 60 fathoms (11-in.) chain and shackles and two (2) stones for buoy here. Can you send by * Senlac ' ?
I endeavoured to send these stones and moorings by the ' Senlac,' but was notified that this could not be done. I then wired the captain February 11. ' Cannot send stones by ' Senlac. Yarmouth Southwest Fairway buoy at Abbott's harbour should be properly secured. Better do this and then return to St. John harbour for gear.'
1 also received a letter from Yarmouth, dated February 10, a copy of which I am attaching.
On the 13th, Capt. Bissett wired me as follows, from Yarmouth: ''Visited Abbott's harbour yesterday, found buoy was secured. Could not turn up candlebox bell-buoy, sea too heavy to-day, strong gales southwest and think proceeding first chance.'
The ' Lansdowne ' then returned to St. John, coaled, took on needed gear, and was ordered to sea on February 19.
Here is a month which was spent for the purpose of locating these buoys which were more important than the one at Old PropTiettor ledge for he reason which I have given to the House.
I am inclosing a copy of my order to the captain. You will note that the Lurcher lightship had to be coaled and then the buoy work was detailed, which had to he attended

to. The Old Proprietor was one of the buoys mentioned in my instructions. The ship did not get away until February 22, and on the 24th the lightship was supplied with coal and all the water she could take.
On February 26 I received a telegram from Yarmouth, as follows: ' Do you wish me to go to the Lurcher lightship No. 15 with pay sheets before handling buoys? Moorings for two buoys on board, weather very bad.' I replied on the same date, ' Want you to tend to buoys first, if weather suitable, you may run over to Lurcher when replacing Yarmouth northwest gas buoy.'
On February 24 the agent at Halifax wired me as follows:	' Blonde Bock buoy drifted,
towed into Wood's harbour. ' Lady Laurier ' going west next trip, can replace unless your ship _ undertaking work. Please advise.'
This telegram was received late in the evening of the 24th, and I answered it on the 25th as follows: ' Will endeavour to replace Blonde Rock buoy, but wish you would order 'Lady Laurier ' to do so, subject my confirmation to her by wireless. Advise me when she leaves.'
I am under the impression that I held conversation over the phone with Mr. Parsons, but at any rate I wired Capt. Bissett on the same date as follows:
' Blonde Bock buoy towed into Wood's harbour, make endeavour to replace before doing Yarmouth Southwest Fairway, as in my opinion Blonde Bock is more important than Southwest Yarmouth.'
Not hearing from Capt. Bissett, I wired him at Yarmouth, March 2, as follows:
' Please advise me where you are, and whether any further work has been done since the Lurcher was supplied with coal.'
Was the Old Proprietor buoy unlighted during all this time?
Yes.
Why did he not give notice to the public that his representation that it would be attended to at once was not being fulfilled?
He did give notice on the 22nd January that the buoy was not lighted.
Did not the public notice state that it would be attended to at once?
As soon as possible.
But a month had gone by without any attempt being made to remedy it.
Yes, because he could not go there. Then he went there, but he could not light the buoy.
Why did he not notify the public?
My hon. friend has missed the point; he could not light it.
It is the minister who has missed the point.

Well, I will read it again:
On January 27 Capt. Bissett wired that the Old Proprietor was in position but the sea was too heavy to light lamp, stated no word of southwest ledge buoy yet.
He went there, but he could not light it.
What was the original notice given to the public?

It was to the effect that Old Proprietor gas or whistling buoy has been reported with light out, and that it will be attended to as soon as possible. He gave instructions immediately. He gave instructions on January 23, February 19, on May 3, and on May 15 to relight the buoy. On May 20 the captain found that he could go near the buov, lout that as the upper part of the buoy was out of order he could not light it. He reported that fact to the agency and he wanted to get a new buoy to replace the old one. There were two spare buoys at that time at St. John, the number that we generally keep there. What happened then? Immediately after that a buoy went adrift from near Brier Island and it had to be replaced immediately by one of these spare buoys. Then, he happened to get a No. 11 buoy and he thought that No. 11 was too heavy. Accordingly he asked that a No. 9 buoy be got. He telephoned Mr. Parsons at Halifax and got a No. 9 buoy. Unfortunately, that buoy had_ no superstructure, so that he had to give instructions to have a superstructure made. That work had to be done at Owen Sound and it took some months to get that superstructure because it is something that is not kept in store by the manufacturers here. Therefore, four months elapsed before he could go near the buoy, and when he saw the buoy he found that it could not be used in the condition in which it was then. He ordered a new buoy, but it took the time I have just mentioned to procure one for this place. The new superstructure arrived about the beginning of September, and it was immediately sent out there. At the same time this same trouble occurred that had occurred before, that is to say, that the buoys of the north-west and southwest ledge of Brier Island went adrift and he had to attend to these. The Lurcher lightship also required attention, and this prevented the ' Lansdowne ' from being able to place the buoy at Old Proprietor ledge before the month of October. These are the main facts which have been brought out by the agent. I could read over this report and the House will see how difficult it is to deal with these buoys in the Bay of Fundy. The tide is very heavy, the winds and gales are very serious, and it is a question whether we should continue the buoys in that section of the Bay of Fundy.

If we were sure that no accidents would happen, well and good, but experience has shown us how difficult it is, especially in winter, to maintain these buoys in the Bay of Fundy. This problem is now engaging the consideration of the departmfent. But to come back to the first point, I would say that if the vessel had followed the proper course, if she had followed the course she should have followed, of making proper soundings or if the officer in charge had taken into consideration the error in his compass I am sure there would be no accident and that the loss of life that we have to deplore to-day would not have occurred.
Now, my hon. friend has found fault with me because Mr. Harding has been removed from the agency at St. John and he says that if Mr. Harding had been there no such accident would have happened. My hon. friend knows the circumstances and I do not know why he brings this question before the House now. It was a painful duty which I had to perform, but in view of the report which has been made by Mr. Justice Cassels no other course was open to me than to superannuate Mr. Harding. I do not need to read the report as doubtless my hon. friend is conversant with it, but Mr. Justice Cassels says this:
No agent can faithfully perform the duties entrusted to liim of letting contracts, supervising works and certifying accounts, &c., where he is under financial obligations to those dealing with him, as representing the department, in the manner described in the evidence.
Mr. Harding was a very sick -man at the time and we had to superannuate him. I think my hon. friend, on giving the matter more consideration, will find that I acted in that case with the utmost justice in regard to Mr. Harding.
Now Mr. Speaker, I do not need to take up further of the time of the House. I think I have answered the accusations which have been made by my hon. friend (Mr. Daniel) against the department and shown that the department cannot be considered at fault under the circumstances. We have done our best to discharge our duty. 1 was not here at the time myself, but of course I am responsible for everything that happened, and I admit there is something that requires fuller information. I am going to get that information and if it is found that some officers have not discharged their duties properly and have not made to the department the reports they should have made I will have to take the steps that a minister should take. I deplore as much as my hon. friend does the serious loss of life; I am probably more sorry than he is, but I think he will render us the justice of saying that the department is doing everything possible to keep these aids to navigation in proper shape so as to give
to navigators proper protection and that in so doing we are discharging our duty to our country.
Is it not usual to give the British Board of Trade notice with regard to aids to navigation?
The only mark shown on this Admiralty chart on the Proprietor rock ledge is a red beacon which is in existence; the gas buoy does not appear on this admiralty chart.
That does not answer the question. Is it not usual to give notice to the British Board of Trade?
I do not know that any notice had been given.

It must be evident to every hon. member who has followed this debate thus far that the Minister of Marine has completely failed to meet the case which has been so clearly and convincingly made out against the department by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Daniel). After all that the minister has said these facts stand out conspicuously uncontroverted: First, that this Old Proprietor buoy was established by the department ostensibly as a necessary protection against this dangerous ledge; secondly, that it was charted so that mariners were led to rely upon it as a guide; thirdly, that the buoy-which was provided, I believe by the department's friend, Mr. Willson, to whom reference has been made by the Civil Service Commission, at a cost of $8,000-was defective; fourthly, that the light went out in January last; fifthly, that the acting agent of the department at St. John inserted an advertisement in three of the St. John newspapers for three days, stating that the light was out and that it would be repaired as soon as possible; sixthly, that no notice was given to the British Board of Trade according to the usual custom and practice so that any mariners other than those under whose notice these local advertisements came were apprised, and as to these latter they were given to understand that it would be repaired as soon as possible; seventhly, the light was allowed to remain out and the buoy to remain defective for nearly ten months; eighthly, that the light was out and the whistle not sounding on the night of the wreck of the ' Hes-tia,' and ninthly and lastly that the ' Hes-tia ' wras wrecked on the very ledge which this buoy was established to protect shipping from. It does seem to me that in view of these facts which stand uncontroverted after the speech of the minister, the department cannot hope to escape responsibility for this lamentable catastrophe. The minister has referred to the findings of the commission which was appointed to investigate this wreck and he relies on these findings

as exonerating the department from all blame. These findings were first, that the wreck was due to an error in the compass, what is called Gauss's error, of which the minister gave the House such an illuminating explanation; second, that there were no soundings taken and that a mistake was made in taking the bearings of Gannet Rock light five miles away. These are the findings upon which the minister relies to excuse the department for all responsibility for this disaster. Do any of these findings touch the questions: That the Old Proprietor buoy was defective, that no notice was given to the British Board of Trade; or do any of them touch the question as to the ten months delay in repairing the buoy? Notwithstanding the local notice which was given by the agent at St. John, not one single thing was done to repair that light and put it in a condition that it could be relied upon as a safe guide to mariners for over nine long months. 'It seems to me that this House has never heard of sucn a flimsy pretext as that given to it by the minister for the non-repair of this buoy. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries wouid have the members of this House believe that for nine months it was impossible because of adverse weather conditions in the Bay of Fundy to repair one of these Willson automatic gas buoys. Was ever a more self-evident arrant absurdity placed before this House and before the public than the statement which the minister placed on ' Hansard ' the other day? As has been pointed out by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Daniel) the weather during the past season in the Bay of Fundy has been perhaps the most favourable that has bem experienced for many years and one cannot believe that during this lengthy period it was impossible for the department to accomplish the repair of this buoy. Then the minister advances another reason for the non-repair of the buoy from January 23, until late in the month of October, and that is that there were other important duties which were engaging the attention of the officers of the department. The minister has read a very long report from Mr. Legere, the acting agent of the department at St. John telling what he had done for the replacement and repair of different lights in different parts of the Bay of Fundy, but it will be observed from the extracts which the minister read from the report that only one effort was made to get to the Old Proprietor buoy and that in the month of January. It is true that the report of the agent which he read showed that the agent of the department was very active in his efforts to find the floating buoys which had been reported adrift in other quarters. But certainly nobody who heard that report can conclude that he took all proper measures to repair this very im-Mr. CROCKET.
portant light at Old Proprietor ledge, the non-repair of which, without any question, was responsible for the disaster which occurred. It may be that the compass was defective, as the minister has endeavoured to make the House believe; but I do not think that he read from the evidence which he had in his hand any testimony which would bear out that statement. The hon. member for the city of St. John this afternoon quoted the testimony given by the witnesses at Montreal, showing that the ' Hestia ' had been swung at Glasgow and the compass tested before she had left that port, and that no material variation had been found. That testimony was given by one of the few surviving officers of the crew. The very fact that the vessel made the Bay of Fundy as she did is pretty strong evidence that the compass was not so defective as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries would have the House believe.
It is quite the reverse. It is because the same course had always been followed; but when the vessel came to change its course, it could not do it properly without having new bearings taken.

Whether the compass was in error or not, what difference does it make as to the liability of the department for the non-repair of the Old Proprietor buoy, the buoy that was placed to pro- . tect vessels from the very rock on which the wreck occurred? The same remark applies to the other findings of the commission and the other grounds advanced by the Minister of Marine as to the failure of the ship's officers to take proper soundings. In that respect also, I think the hon. member for the city of St. John read this afternoon evidence that soundings had been taken, and also evidence with reference to the taking of the bearings of Gannet Rock light, a light which was five miles distant from the scene of this wreck. It seems to me that none of these facts excuse the Department of Marine and Fisheries from liability or responsibility for this wreck. To my mind it admits of no manner of doubt that had that light been working, and had he whistle been sounding as it should have been, on the night of this wreck, the wreck would not have occurred; and in that view, I think it is impossible for any unbiassed mind to acquit the department of responsibility as the minister has sought to induce the House to do. It did seem to me that the excuse advanced about the officers of the department being engaged with more important business was one which under the circumstances the officers of the department should have refrained from putting upon the records of this House. I understand, from the statement which the minister has made, that the other more important business referred

to was the looking after the other buoys and aids to navigation at the other points in the Bay of Fundy that he mentioned. But, Sir, when one recalls the pitiful cries of the poor -little boy from Scotland, to whom the hon. member for St. John made reference, within a few hours of his destination, 1 Mother, save me, I am drowning/ and when one thinks of the fearful scenes which were enacted m the darkness of that cold and stormy night, when thirty-nine precious lives were sacrificed to, what I think has been clearly shown to have been the neglect of this department, one wonders at the callousness and the heartlessness of the officers of the department in putting such a statement as that upon the records of this House: ' other more important business on hand/ Mr. Speaker, it was not long ago when a Royal Commission appointed by this government exposed to the people of this country the inefficiency, the incompetence and the corruption which characterized the administration of this department. That commission exposed those conditions in very strong language which will not soon be forgotten. But I venture to say that those conditions which characterize this department have been brought home to the people of the maritime provinces at least, by this lamentable disaster and loss of life with an effect which no language, however strong, can produce, and which no such sophistry as the Minister of Marine has addressed to this House to-night will alter.

Mr. Speaker, as the House has been occupied for several hours in the discussion of this resolution, which has been moved by the hon. member for the city of St. John (Mr. Daniel), I feel it fitting on my part that I should say a few words in regard to this wreck. Representing the county in which these waters are, and in which the Old Proprietor ledge is situated, I feel that it is due to my constituency that I should say a few words on this subject. The hon. member for the city of St. John, followed by the hon. member for the county of York (Mr. Crocket), would lead this House to believe that almost a murder had been laid at the doors of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. There is nothing whatever in the evidence to justify such blame being placed upon the department, I think the blame for the wreck should be rather placed upon the captain and the other officers of the ship. Any one who looks at the map of the coast of the Bay of Fundy, with its high tides and the small opening at the mouth, will understand that there is naturally a great current in that water. He will also see that from Brier Island light to the light at Gannet rock, two of the best lights in this country, there is a breadth of nearly thirty miles of water, in which this 11
ship was fully nine miles out of her course. So that I believe the judgment of this House will bear me out in saying that there must have been something vitally wrong with the compass of that ship. It is said by the hon. member for the City of St. John (Mr. Daniel) that the compass was tested when the vessel left the other side, and he asked if the vessel was so much out of her course on account of a defect in the compass, how she could have found the mouth of the Bay of Fundy. Well, she was only nine miles out of her course, and still there was an opening of thirty miles between Brier Island and Gannet Rock light. It is altogether too fine a point to pretend that if the gas buoy of Old Proprietor ledge was not working, that was sufficient reason for the captain of the ' Hestia ' paying no attention to Gannet Rock light and changing his bearings and shifting his course.
I regret that the hon. member for the city of St. John (Mr. Daniel) in his anxiety to make a point against the government, should have cast reflections on the shipping facilities of his own city. We are all trying to build up a winter port in the great city of St. John. Have we not heard over and over again in years past from our sister provinces and the other side of the water that the Bay of Fundy is a tortuous, difficult course for vessels? Should not the hon. member for St. John city rather uphold the advantages of the Bay of Fundy than decry them? I think he would be doing his duty by his constituency much better by urging this government to build up the harbour and equip it with better lights and every protection possible. But instead, he appeals to the House, followed by the hon. member for York (Mr. Crocket), and with tears in his voice he repeats the-cries of the two Scotch boys who met a watery grave. One of them, he said, in his last moments, as he sank below the water exclaimed in agony: Mother, save us. But as a medical man, has my hon. friend not often heard that cry for help from patients drifting towards the rocks of Eternity? And because he as medical adviser could not save them, are w'e expected to hold him responsible for their death? I think it would better become the hon. gentleman and the hon. member for York (Mr. Crocket) to work for the improvement of the harbour of St. John and the better equipment of the Bay of Fundy with aids to navigation than try to arouse prejudice and belittle their own port approaches as they are doing. I would suggest to the Minister of Marine that instead of trying to establish a lighthouse as requested by the hon. member for St. John, he should have , a submarine bell, placed in 10 fathoms of water near the Old Proprietor ledge and an electric light on the spindle



on said ledge, connected and worked from White Head Island, by the proper cable. This in my opinion, and that of many living near to this dangerous reef, would remove all danger to vessels or steamers at this point.

This subject has been so thoroughly debated that very little remains to be said. I do not think it will do for the minister to take the ground that he and his department are absolutely absolved by any amount of censure cast upon the captain and the officers who are no longer alive to defend themselves. Whether or not the compass was out, whether or not the captain took sufficient soundings, it is perfectly clear that this wreck would not. have occurred and these lives would not have, been lost if that light had been in proper working order. I do not think any one who has listened to the minister and who has read the reports in the public press could entertain the slightest doubts on that point. True the gentleman who acted as chairman of this board of inquiry took the ground that no great reliance should be placed on these floating lights and Captain Gillies, the superintendent of the Donaldson line, retorted that certainly no one would rely in the future upon floating lights in Canadian waters. But it seems rather peculiar that the course of events should have been what it was. This light became extinct about the 22nd of January, 1909. A notice was sent- not apparently in the ordinary course so that it would reach the mariners -but was pubilished in the local newspapers in the city of St. John. I do not know whether Captain Gillies was correct in the observation he made that no navigator would hereafter rely on our floating lights, but I did observe that in the course of the inquiry he said that no official notice had been given the mariners with regard to it. The minister will know best whether or not that statement was correct. Capt. Lugar, the chairman, remarked:
But the fact that the light was not burning was published in all the Halifax newspapers.
To which Captain Gillies replied: Perhaps, but not in the official notification issued to the mariners by the government.
Even if it had been published in those official notifications, one would suppose that the department, finding that the light could not be replaced within reasonable time, would have given timely notice in some official communication so that it would have reached the mariners; but for ten months that light was absolutely extinct and no more notice given of that important fact than the notice published in the local newspapers.
These new gas buoys were heralded by the Department of Marine and Fisheries as Mr. TODD.
a most important advance. To such an extent did this go that on January 31, 1906, the deputy minister of the department gave a certificate to the United States government with regard to them. According to the report of the Civil Service Commission, that certificate was in these words:
This department has had in the past considerable difficulty in carrying out its policy of providing an efficient buoy lighting system and has taken great pains to test and investigate the Willson buoy, with the result that it has been fully adopted; and the department purchases no other types. It is regarded as a distinct improvement on all others which the department has used. I can therefore recommend it to your Board.
This was a most distinct and unqualified recommendation of this buoy from the Department of Marine and Fisheries of Canada to the government of the United States. This efficiency comes to be tested in a portion of the Bay of Fundy that is regarded as having a special need of every possible aid to navigation that can be devised. The light goes out on January 22, 1909. Perhaps the minister can state when the buoy was placed there?
I could not state exactly, I suppose two or three years ago.

I suppose it had been tested before being placed there, yet it goes out and as I understand the whistling apparatus also becomes defective and for a period of nine months both those defects remain absolutely without any remedy or correction. I would not say that this is an efficient buoy for the purpose unless it is of such a character that it can be repaired within a reasonable time and unless the materials and means for repairing it within a reasonable time are available, because, as Captain Gillies very well says, it would be far better to have no light at all than to place a light there and allow it to go out without giving any notice to mariners, the natural reliance on the light, operates as a complete and perfect trap to navigators who are traversing that portion of the Bay of Fundy.
I am not very much concerned with the fine-spun theories about the compass which have been enlarged upon by the minister and to which so much importance has been attached by Capt. Lugar. I think it would not be possible to arrive at any correct conclusion on that subject unless we had the evidence of the captain and officers of the ship who are now no longer here to testify. As far as the taking of soundings is concerned, it is evident from the testimony that soundings were taken as late as 11.30 o'clock that night.

Some soundings were taken during the day on the south coast

of Nova Scotia, but he did not take any soundings when near the rocks.

Soundings were taken every half hour according to the evidence of one of the officers, he himself reading the log after each sounding. A sounding was taken about 11.30 p.m., when the depth of water was 100 fathoms.
They continued two hours after that without soundings.

Those soundings were taken at least as late as 11.30 p.m., and it would seem inconceivable under the circumstances, with the condition of the weather and the position in which the vessel was, that the captain would cease taking soundings when he had taken them every half hour up to that time.
I see that Captain Lugar has rejected what would seem to me to be important evidence. On the dead body of one of the seamen, who was steering the ship, was found a memorandum indicating the course he was steering, a written statement of the course he was directed to steer. I would consider that good evidence, I think it would be received in a court of law and why Captain Lugar, chairman of the board, should have seen fit to reject that evidence is not very clear to me. Further than that, counsel for the steamship company asked especially that as the causes of the wreck were being investigated the Court of Inquiry should be adjourned to St. John. N.B., where men familiar with all the local conditions might be summoned to give evidence in order to make the result of the investigation more accurate and more clear. I do not see why that course was not pursued. The evidence of the survivors of the crew had been taken; the object was to discover the cause of the accident and the wreck, and when counsel for the steamship company asked that the court should be adjourned to a locality near where the accident had occurred, where men familiar with these tides which have been enlarged upon, men familiar with all the difficulties of navigation, could be summoned and might have thrown some light on the subject, the chairman airily put the request aside and said there was no occasion to take any such course. Does the minister approve of that course? Does he not think that some light might have been thrown on the circumstances attending this wreck by adopting that course? I am putting altogether aside the conduct of those on shore and dealing only with the causes of the wreck. It does seem clear that some light might have been thrown on the circumstances of the case by calling men familiar with the difficulties and the navigation of those waters.
The minister has spoken of insurance rates and has deprecated in a mild way the 114
discussion of these matters in the House of Commons. The tone and spirit in which my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Daniel) introduced this subject in the House indicated a sincere desire on his part to do only that which was in the public interest and in no way to create prejudice or cast discredit on the navigation of these waters. As far as that is concerned, I think the circumstances brought out in the inquiry, the fact that this buoy remained ten months unlighted and with its whistling apparatus out of order, would do much more to cast discredit on navigation in the Bay of Fundy than anything that could possibly be said in this House.
I do trust that the minister will not permit the matter to remain in its present position, that a further inquiry will be had and tljat he will be able to come down to the House later on and give us some assurance as to the continuous efficiency of these buoys. One of the chief causes he has urged to the House in defence of the inconceivable delay of nine months in repairing this buoy is the fact that so many other buoys had got out of order and gone adrift. Something must be wrong. Either the buoys are not adapted for the waters of that coast, cannot properly be secured; or are otherwise inefficient, or else there is some neglect on the part of some official of the department. The two things cannot stand together. If the buoys are of the proper type, if they can be made fast, if they are efficient and if the officials of the department do their duty then no such condition of affairs could have occurred in those waters as that which the minister himself has exposed to the House this evening in making his defence in this matter. I sincerely trust that some further inquiry will be held and further explanation will be given and that those who are interested in the navigation of Canadian waters will be able to understand that the course which has been pursued and the conditions which have arisen in this matter are not likely to occur again.

I have listened very carefully to the speech of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and I cannot at all agree that he has made it clear that the acting agent did his duty in this matter. He read a long report from the acting agent. But that report, as I understood it, and as I heard it read, only accounted for four or five months of the year, and stated what he was busy about during those months. But there was a long hiatus between the end of the four months and the end of the nine months. What was he doing the other five months after he had been so busy during these first four months? I also noticed the fact that when the Fairway buoy at Yarmouth got adrift he notified the Board of Trade. Why, Sir, when this buoy went

wrong, if the agent of the department, _ or the department itself, had taken the action which they should have taken, and had sent an official notification to mariners, then I say the negligence of the department in taking nine months and more to remedy the defects of this buoy, would not have been so reprehensible, in fact would not have been reprehensible to any extent, because they would have discharged their . duty and notified the mariners, sea captains and others that when they came into these waters they could not expect to find that Old Proprietor buoy.
The acting agent did better than that, he notified the owners, the agents of the ' Hestia.'

He gave verbal notice to the agent of the Donaldson line. 4
Mr. PUGSLEY Of this very line.

Yes, of this very line, in January, nine months ago. And what was that notification? A notification to the effect that the buoy was adrift, or the light was out, and that the defect would be remedied as soon as possible. So when it comes to the fall of the year, October or November, had not those captains, those mariners, those navigators, a right to suppose that the defect had been remedied long ago? That is the point of the whole matter-the fact that not only was this defect allowed to continue, but that those who ought to have been acquainted with the fact were not put in possession of it, or still worse, that the notification given was a deceptive one, as it only stated that the buoy was adrift, or the light out, and that the defect would be remedied as soon as possible. Now there is one point in the minister's speech that I was glad to hear, when he says that he intends to have a further investigation. I think it is absolutely necessary to have a further investigation, and I hope that investigation will be thorough and rigid, and cover all these points with regard to which evidence is so necessary, namely, the need of life saving stations and crews, of life boats, the quality of life boat and all those needs in the Bay of Fundy. The minister also spoke about the difficulty of keeping the buoys in a certain place in the Bay of Fundy, and he said he was considering whether the department ought to continue to keep those buoys going. My opinion, formed from the evidence that was given at this investigation, is that it is far better to have no buoys at all than to have buoys listed and put on the chart, and then when you come to the place where you expect to find them, they are either adrift, or there is no light, or whistle or anything of that kind. Such a thing as that" is simply a lure to destruc-Mr. DANIEL.
tion. Far better to have no buoys at all on those exposed positions than to expect them and then find nothing there when you get there. That is the complaint we have to make.
Now before I sit down I want to refer to a remark made by the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Todd). The hon. member for Charlotte reproached me because I made a reference to a disaster in the Bay of Fundy and had drawn the attention of the country to the fact that the Department of Marine had been remiss in its duty in looking after the lights at the Old Proprietor rock. Sir, when he was saying that he reminded me of a bird, I believe a very stupid bird, an inhabitant of South Africa. That bird, when it is pursued and wants to hide itself, simply buries its head in the hush or in the ground, and thinks that because it cannot see any one no one can see it. That appears to me to be the position the hon. member for Charlotte would like me to take. He wants me to say nothing about this, to conceal it, and he thinks that then nobody else will know anything about it. But if we were to take that course the defect would never be remedied. That_ is not the position I take. I take the position that the proper course to take under these circumstances is to make this thing so public that it will never occur again, that the department will act in a more rigid and conscientious manner in future than it has been doing in the past, and then the navigation up and down the bay to and from the city I have the honour to represent, will be safer than it ever has been in the past.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: TRADE MISSION TO JAPAN OF W. T. R.
TRADE MISSION TO JAPAN OF W. T. R.
speechtext:
MONK (Jacques Cartier), moved:
For a copy of all correspondence, petitions, reports and written representations in tlie hands of the government, or any department of the same, concerning the commercial or trade mission to Japan of W. T. R. Preston, as Canadian Trade Commissioner for Canada, and of the report of said commissioner, as well as all other reports and despatches received by the government in connection with the execution of said mission.
He said: The object of this motion is to bring before the House all the correspondence that has taken place between the government and Mr. Preston, as well as between the government and any persons in Japan, or between the government and the British ambassador, or any representative of other governments in Japan, during the execution of the mission confided to Mr. Preston by the government. I think that

correspondence will prove very interesting and instructive. As I understand the events that have taken place since Mr. Preston went to Japan, he was entrusted with the mission of opening up direct relations between the commercial houses in Japan, the commercial rvorld generally of Japan, and our own people, in order to establish direct trade relations between the two countries, in consequence of the treaty which was recently concluded between Japan and Great Britain, our adhesion, in other words, to the treaty concluded by Great Britain with Japan some ten or twelve years ago.
From what I have been able to cull from the newspapers, what has been published since Mr. Preston "went to Japan and since his return, that mission was altogether marred, or came to very little, and the circumstances appear to be as follows:	It
would seem that in Japan, since that country has endeavoured to develop commercial relations with occidental countries all over this part of the world a certain number of commission merchants have established themselves in Japan and they have succeeded in implanting there a system by which all commercial relations must take place through themselves. They object to any direct relations and they have sedulously spread all over the world the idea that the Japanese commercial houses are not to be trusted but that through them and only through them can safe commercial relations be had with the Japanese merchants. Of course, the arrival there of Mr. Preston under the circumstances was anything but welcomed. He was considered as an intruder, arriving there presumably for the purpose of breaking up this system that existed in Japan. But, he was welcomed by the Japanese. The Japanese merchants are anxious to develop direct commercial relations with Canada and with all parts of the world. They are people with whom commercial relations can be safely maintained just as well as with other people and the moment Mr. Preston began there the execution of his mission and endeavoured to establish direct relations-between the commercial men of Japan and Canada he became, so to speak, the butt of the attacks of these commission houses and, as far as my information goes, these commission houses, being- confined principally to English and American firms, solicited the intervention of the British ambassador to cause Mr. Preston to cease his campaign. I understand that the correspondence will show that. Correspondence took place between His Majesty's representative in Japan and the Canadian government either directly or through the Home government. I am not sure as to that, but it has been stated in the papers that the claim was made on behalf of the English commission houses that Mr. Preston was interfering with their business,
that he was disturbing commercial security and solidity in Japan and that it was desirable that he should be recalled. I think that is a point of very great importance upon which the House should be very fully informed. I have reason to believe that the objections from the commission houses, not only the English commission houses, but others as well, were forwarded to the Canadian government or to the imperial government, to be, by them, communicated to the Canadian government. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) will probably know whether these allegations are well founded or not, but steps of various kinds were taken in order to secure the recall of Mr. Preston and his mission there was not only interfered with but was nullified by the influence that I have just referred to. This information has come to me from the newspapers and I think it is very important that the House should see that correspondence that we may know exactly what Mr. Preston did there and what his reports stated as to the possibilities of establishing direct trade communication with that nation, because there is no doubt that we have an immense possible commerce not only with Japan but with all those Asiatic countries. We are therefore interested to know why that mission was brought abruptly to a close and what was the result of the mission itself. I think it is even more important why we should know why that mission came to an end, what were exactly the influences which were brought to bear, the representations that were made against or for Mr. Preston by the associated interests, by those commission houses established there and on his behalf by other commercial bodies, chambers of commerce and Japanese interested in his mission. I think the idea is covered by my motion. I have prepared a motion somewhat longer but I mislaid it. The motion that I had originally prepared after I had seen this matter formulated in the newspapers was to this effect:
Copy of the correspondence between the Department of Trade and Commerce and the late Commissioner of Trade in Japan, Mr. Preston, on all subjects arising out of the controversy between Mr. Preston and foreign commission merchants in Japan during and subsequent to his stay there.
Copy of correspondence between the government of Canada and the British Ambassador in Japan respecting or in any way relating to Mr. Preston's appointment to Japan, the discharge of his duties there or connected with the controversy arising in Japan from Mr. Preston's advocacy of direct trade between Canadians and Japanese.
Copy of correspondence between the government of Canada, the British and the United States and the German Ambassadors and Mr. Preston on subjects growing out of the advocacy of direct trade between Canada and Japan.
Copy of all correspondence, loose paper clippings, memorials from Japanese or For-

eign Chambers of Commerce in Japan, or with the Colonial Office in London, touching or relating to the subject matter referred to herein.
I may say to the House that although it seems to me that it is covered by the motion I gave notice of this one is fuller and may be substituted for that which appears on the notice paper if the House will admit of the substitution. As I am informed Mr. Preston was actually recalled. I do not believe that the reason of that recall was that he was not carrying on properly his commercial mission, but that he had fallen upon a mare's nest there, had stirred up a great deal of trouble, and that, in reality, it was that opposition to the execution of his mission which brought about his recall -all the more reason why the House ought to be fully informed of all the circumstances. I understand also that since Mr. Preston's return, or simultaneously with his recall, another commissioner, a Mr. Harris, w*as named to replace him. It is stated in the newspapers that Mr. Harris rather inclines to the views, or falls in with the ideas, of those who think that direct commercial relations with that country are difficult because it has been stated in the public press that Mr. Harris has written a letter from Japan to a commercial house here stating in effect that the Japanese, in matters of business, are not to be trusted. That is what the newspapers state is the purport of his letter. Then there would be an absolute contradiction between the representations and reports made by Mr Preston and the statement or representation made by the new appointee. A newspaper has stated that in that statement which he communicated to a commercial house here the new representative had not the support of the government. All this, it seems to me, is rather confusing and it would be very interesting for us to have the whole of the papers before us because this is a singular case that has never, to my knowledge, come to the notice of the government since we attempted to establish direct relations and I think the House will find some interesting data if these papers are all brought down. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I will substitute this rather longer motion hut in effect it is the same as that on the Order Paper.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TRADE MISSION TO JAPAN OF W. T. R.
speechtext:
I am not sufficiently acquainted with the matters to which my hon. friend has referred to justify me in making a reply to his observations. I quite realize that the matter is a proper one for inquiry and I would have no objection to the notice which appears on the Order Paper. It may be that on further consideration we would have no objection to the motion he now presents, but if my hon. friend thinks there is a substantial difference between the two I would suggest that he drop the motion on the Order Paper and substitute the Mr. MONK.
other by way of notice. If the motion on the Order Paper is substantially what he wants I think he had better take it and any papers dealing with the matter which can properly be brought down will be produced at an early date.

subtopic: TRADE MISSION TO JAPAN OF W. T. R.
speechtext: I am induced to accept the suggestion of the Minister of Finance because I understand there are a considerable number of papers and I do not want to have delay. Did I understand the hon. gentleman to say that some of these papers might not properly be brought down, and if so I would remark that this is not a confidential or state matter and that none of the papers relating to it can very well be withheld.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TRADE MISSION TO JAPAN OF W. T. R.
speechtext: I do not wish to indicate that to my knowledge there are any papers that should not be brought down, and my remark was intended only to put in the usual general saving clause. I am not unmindful that in international matters it frequently arises that there are some papers that cannot be brought down. It was with that general thought in my mind, and not with any particular reference to these papers, that I made this remark.
Motion agreed to.

Public Works Department, salaries, $358,537.50.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext: Six additional employees in the department are provided for next year. The total increase in salaries is $5,182, which is largely made up of the salaries of these six officials and the statutory increases to the others.
Are there any who did not receive the statutory increases?

Not in the first division, they are all entitled to it in that division. Mr. J. A. Robillard, Mr. J. A. Blain, Mr. G. M. Hutchinson, and Mr. G. Perley are promoted from the second division (subdivision A) to the first division of subdivision B. Then there is Louis Coste, who was in this division, and who has been transferred to the outside service. My hon. friend will know that he is connected with the International Waterways Commission.
What is his salary?
$25 per day during the time he is actually engaged in the services of the government. In the 2nd division, subdivision ' A,' there are twenty-three statutory increases at $50.
Were any of the officers of the 1st division, subdivision ' B/.not given the statutory increase?
Yes, there are apparently two.
Why not?

Because they were not recommended as entitled to receive it. Under the Civil Service Act it is optional with the deputy minister to recommend them or not. In the 2nd division, subdivision 'A,' there are twenty-three statutory increases at $50, four at $25, and one at $12.50, making a total of $1,262.50. There are seven promotions from subdivision ' B ' to division 'A' of the 2nd division. This makes a total of $14,062.50. From this is to be deducted the salaries of four employees promoted from the first division, subdivision ' B,' the salary of Mr. Lucas who resigned, and half the salary of Mr. McLaughlin, which was paid by the Railways and Canals Department, a total of $10,025, leaving an increase in this subdivision of $4,037.50.
How many in this division were passed over without getting the increase?
Four.
Have the promotions been made on the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission?
They will have to be made in the report of the Civil Service Commission that they are entitled thereto.
Are they proposed promotions or have the promotions already been made?
They are proposed promotions.
Are they made as the result of competitive examinations?

No, the promotions are not made as the result of competitive examination, except in the lower division. They are made on the recommendation of the deputy minister and the certificate of the commission that the persons recommended are qualified to be promoted.
Are there any new appointments in that department?
Two or three are contemplated.
Are they to be appointed on the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission?

Yes, they will have to be, unless of course officials are promoted from a lower division, in which case there would be vacancies in the lower division to which appointments would have to be made on the recommendation of the commission. In the 2nd division, subdivision 'B,' there are forty-seven statutory increases at $50 and four at $25, and there are to be two promotions.
Who are they?

Dostaler and T. G. Bell. In the third division, subdivision 'A,' there are twenty-three statutory increases at $50 and one at $25, and there are to be nine promotions from subdivision ' B ' to subdivision ' A.' There are some reductions and some transfers, making a total increase in that division of $4,900.
Let us have the names of those promoted.

Miss M: E. Sylvain, V. Lepage, C. A. Narraway, Miss A. Valade, Mrs. M. L. Roy, M. Laframboise, F. O. Hamel, J. E. Kennedy and A. A. Rivard. In the third division, subdivision ' B,' there are three statutory increases at $50, and seven at $25.
Does the minister designate those who -are proposed for promotion, or how comes he to have their names there?

They are proposed subject to the certificate of the commission. There is a new appointment in this division-Miss McPherson, who was appointed after examination and on the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission.
Has the Civil Service Commission recommended for promotion those whose names the minister has read?
These are what the deputy minister believes are the proper promotions. All the commission has to do is to certify that the parties are qualified for promotion.
I presume the commission will be pliable.
If the initiative is not taken by the. Civil Service Commission with regard to competitive examination, what is the advantage of this over the old system?
No new appointment, except in some special cases, can be made to the service except upon competitive examination and the recommendation of the commissioners.
No advantage with regard to promotion.
No, except that they must certify that the person whom the deputy recommends is qualified.
Does the hon. minister find that those appointed by the Civil Service Commission are much better than those appointed in the good old way oi political pull. I must say I believe in the old way.

I must say I was not here when, the good old way prevailed.

Who is the officer to be-promoted?

We contemplate the promotion of Mr. Saunders who has been in the office for many years.
Department of Mines, salaries, $174,689.
Does the government intend establishing an institution for the better testing and reducing of ores?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is contemplated by the director of mines to have a plant in Ottawa. The building is being erected. Possibly the production of gas from peat will be tested the coming summer. To what extent we wiil go in providing plant for the testing of ores is a moot question, but we are not losing sight of it.
Has the hon. gentleman's officers taken notice of the possibility of using peat exhaust or coal in what is termed suction gases or producer gases?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is being investigated. An officer leaves in a day or two to visit an experimental plant in New Jersey for the purpose of acquiring information and he will make a report. The total increases in civil government over last year is $19,675, made up of statutory increases $3,625, increases by promotions $1,450, additional- appointments $14,600. We have an additional clerk in the department proper, an additional mining engineer in the mines branch and a statistical clerk. In the geological survey, two additional geologists at $2,100 each and two draughtsmen at $1,200 each. The total increase in the number of officers for the next financial year is 10.
Has the minister lost any of his geological survey officers in recent years?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes, we are losing one at the present moment.
And the minister knows why?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: With the concurrence and approval of the Civil Service Commission, I propose to recommend these increases by promotion to council. In this way we propose to increase the salaries of half a dozen of the senior geologists.
Does not the minister think the salaries he pays to his first-class officers are not adequate to retain good men?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Quite true. In the Geological Survey we have half a dozen geologists who have served from 25 to 35 years They are in subdivision B of the first division, the maximum of which class is $2,800 The geologist who is likely to leave us now has been thirty odd years in the service. He is receiving $2,300 or $2,400 and he has been offered $4,000 to take charge of the Mines branch of the province of Quebec. While he was reluctant to sever his connection with the department where he would be entitled to superannuation in a few years and where he was carrying on congenial work, we were unable to offer him a larger salary at the moment, but his name is here as one of those proposed to be promoted in the event of his not accepting this position in Quebec. His increase would be $460 to bring him into subdivision A where he would go up from $2,800 to $4,000. 1 desire to put all six of the senior geologists into subdivision A of the first division where they will ultimately go to $4,000. It is absolutely impossible for the Department of Mines to retain well qualified technical men unless we can pay them larger salaries. We have lost half a dozen men who have gone to private enterprises and it is for the purpose of giving fairly adequate salaries that this increase is made. In providing for these additional positions, we are anxious to have the vacancies so that we may secure good men if opportunity presents itself.
Department of the Secretary of State, salaries, $56,412.50.

There is a decrease here of $1,375 due to the transfer of one of the officers and the death of another. These vacancies will be filled by new appointments at the minimum salaries of the divisions.
Department of External Affairs, $14,875.

It will be observed that the number of officials has been increased by four, comprising three clerks in the lowest division and one messenger. The work of the department has increased to such an extent that, it will be necessary to make these appointments in the lowest division and also to secure a messenger.
Who is the head of this department?
Mr. Joseph Pope.
Will these appointments be made as the result of the Civil Service examinations?
Yes.
Who is the officer in subdivision A?
That is Mr. Walker, transferred from the Governor General's office.
Who is the next one in subdivision B?
Mr. Brophy.
Does this department make any report?

The department was only organized on the 1st of June last. It will make a report.
Some resolutions reported.
